title: Tor Hides Your IP, Not Your Words: Free LLMs as an Attribute-Inference Threat to Users of Network Anonymity Tools
abstract: Tor and VPNs hide a user's IP address, and users often treat that as anonymity. We show that the text such users post remains a strong source of personal information, and that extracting it is now free. On 100 synthetic authors from the SynthPAI dataset, two free-tier Gemini models inferred eight personal attributes from the authors' comments. The best model guessed sex correctly 85.4% of the time, occupation 71.4% and country 72.3%, with a mean of 64.3% over all attributes; most of these attributes are never revealed by an IP address at all. A simple defense, rewriting comments with an LLM before posting, lowered mean accuracy to 49.5% but did not remove any attribute. We release all code and raw model outputs.

title: linlog
abstract: A linear logic suite: a Rust library and a command line program that decide, check, prove step by step and export sequents of classical and intuitionistic linear logic and their fragments, keep proofs in a form an independent checker validates, show them as derivation trees or proof nets, and decide ordinary propositional logic through its embeddings into linear logic. Its code, tests and documentation were written with substantial AI assistance, by Anthropic's Claude models in Claude Code, in steps the author planned, directed and accepted, and the author is responsible for them. Its results do not rest on the model that wrote it: every proof it returns is validated by an independent proof checker, classical proofs can be exported as certificates that the Rocq proof assistant checks, the tests are measured by mutation testing and fuzzing, and its verdicts on published problem libraries are compared with their known status and with those of eight other provers.

title: Structure-prior relation graph learning for spatio-temporal anomaly detection in multi-entity collaborative systems
abstract: Spatio-temporal anomaly detection in multi-entity collaborative systems aims to identify abnormal states from multivariate time series generated by dynamically coupled variables. Fully data-driven relation learning may recover unstable or spurious dependencies when normal observations are limited, noisy, or weakly informative about rare coordination failures. This paper studies structure-prior relation graph learning (SPRGL), which augments a GDN-style predictive graph backbone with weak structural priors. Variable groups, topology files, or process connectivity are represented as a structure-prior graph and united with the embedding-derived candidate graph before graph-attention prediction. The technical contribution is therefore the candidate-edge fusion mechanism, rather than the established embedding, Top- k graph learning, attention forecasting, or residual-scoring components. We also construct CTown-RB as a semi-synthetic benchmark containing five injected relation-breaking scenarios based on public CTown topology and normal BATADAL operating data. Under the reported comparison with PCA-SPE, Isolation Forest, and LOF, SPRGL obtains the highest reported F1 and AUC-PR in the SMD, BATADAL, and CTown-RB settings shown in Table 1 ; a separate HAI experiment examines sensitivity to the residual-aggregation size k s . On CTown-RB, the combined prior changes PA-F1 from 0.5651 to 0.8734 and detects all five injected scenarios, while also reducing Precision. These results delimit the current evidence to the reported baselines, datasets, and archived evaluation outputs.

title: When Do Latent World Models Detect Game Glitches? Representation Collapse, Pretrained Video Latents, and an Action-Conditioned Benchmark
abstract: Latent world models trained only on normal gameplay are an appealing, label-free source of "surprise" for glitch detection. This article extends our conference diagnostic study, which found that a LeWorldModel-style JEPA trained from scratch on TempGlitch collapses to effective rank ≈ 1 and reaches AUROC 0.579–0.588, clearly below a kNN detector on frozen VideoMAE features (0.6895). We add three pieces of evidence. (i) Frozen V-JEPA 2 latents. A kNN detector on frozen V-JEPA 2 features reaches 0.6592, and a normal-only next-latent predictor on its 0.4 s temporal tokens reaches 0.665–0.669, a statistical tie with, but not above, VideoMAE kNN; a causal transformer predictor on the same tokens is worse (0.598–0.599). (ii) Collapse remedies. In a pre-specified six-arm sweep (SIGReg weight, batch size, VICReg terms, longer training; one seed), the LeWM encoder's effective rank rises from 1.13 to 21.3, but AUROC does not follow: the best arm (batch 32) reaches 0.6264 (+0.0427 over the reproduced anchor, p = 0.00076), whereas the least-collapsed arm reaches 0.5954 (arm-level Spearman ρ = 0.37, n = 6). (iii) An action-conditioned benchmark. We build ACGB, five headless games with recorded per-frame actions, eight programmatic glitch types at three severities, and a counterfactual clean twin per glitched episode. On its development split, action conditioning does not help the JEPA (macro AUROC 0.605 with actions vs. 0.625 without) but does help a small pixel predictor (0.888 vs. 0.783), notably on input-remapping glitches; locked-test results are pending. (iv) A surprise-driven explorer. On 400 held-out bugged levels with state-triggered hidden bugs, an agent maximising world-model surprise finds fewer bugs than random actions (found fraction 0.258 vs. 0.322) and raises about fifteen times more false alarms on clean levels. Across all experiments, non-collapse is necessary but not sufficient: the temporal content of the latent space matters more than its rank.

title: The Diodic Search Architecture: Regex Search without Per-File Metadata Cost
abstract: We present a prepared-corpus regex search system that reduces repeated-query latency by amortizing per-file filesystem metadata costs into a one-time packing and indexing phase. A SIMD candidate filter reduces exact-match work but introduces no false negatives. On stable corpora with many small files the system achieves substantial end-to-end speedups — 2.79–3.38× over ripgrep 15 on a fixed 20,000-file corpus and 6.66–12.41× on a live 95,942-file, 1.94 GB registry across the patterns whose result sets coincide, breaking even at Q* ≈ 24 queries — and the advantage diminishes for one-shot searches or frequently changing corpora. An in-process timer reports a phantom 53.9% win for a leaked unmap that the external wall clock refuses, and every end-to-end performance claim in this paper rests on external wall-clock measurements; the in-process timings are reported separately as diagnostics, for the segments they explain and nothing more. Count parity holds on every comparison reported here except the two live-registry patterns marked † in Table 11, where the store returned a strict subset of the direct engine’s answer; no ratio is claimed for them, and both endpoints of the registry range come from coinciding patterns. Even there the store arm of that snapshot did not extract container text, so the range is a property of that historical configuration — the missing work could have lowered the store’s cost without changing its answer — and this paper reports no full-pipeline registry measurement. The Tesla valve serves as an architectural inspiration for asymmetric cost, not as a physical model or performance explanation. Preprint — not peer reviewed; comments welcome. Manuscript dated October 18, 2026. Source code: https://github.com/danalec/rgx

title: CorrCLIPv2: Harnessing Unlabeled Images for Open-Vocabulary Semantic Segmentation
abstract: Open-vocabulary semantic segmentation aims to classify pixels without being restricted to a fixed set of categories. Although Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training (CLIP) demonstrates remarkable potential for open-vocabulary recognition, its segmentation capability is impaired by noisy inter-class patch interactions. To this end, this work proposes a unified training-free object-centric framework, named CorrCLIPv2, from three complementary aspects of patch correlation, feature representation, and output regularization. Specifically, for patch correlation, we leverage class-agnostic mask generators to explicitly disentangle inter-class interactions. Moreover, we utilize spatially-coherent features from self-supervised models to compute attention scores to mitigate mask inaccuracies. Regarding feature representation, we devise a refinement mechanism to simultaneously strengthen spatial details and semantic representation. Within the output space, we unify predictions via voting in each mask to enhance spatial consistency. To mitigate contextual bias and enhance prediction accuracy of objects, we further extend the framework by incorporating a cross-image object retrieval paradigm, which incurs minimal computational overhead. We build a memory bank of CorrCLIP-enhanced features from unlabeled images and implement a regime of multi-CLIP ensemble. By aggregating semantically consistent object features across diverse contexts retrieved from the memory bank, CorrCLIPv2 mitigates context-induced interference and obtains more robust predictions. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our approach establishes a new state-of-the-art on 10 standard benchmarks. Remarkably, it even surpasses fully supervised open-vocabulary methods across 22 multi-domain datasets. Code is available at: https://github.com/zdk258/CorrCLIP.

title: Goal Images Are Control Targets: Spatially-Grounded Goal-Image Synthesis for Robotic Manipulation
abstract: Goal-conditioned manipulation policies are steered by a goal image, a picture of the desired post-manipulation scene synthesized from the current observation and a language instruction. The prevailing assumption is that better image-editing quality yields better goals, so goal generators are built and compared using general image-editing metrics. We show this assumption is false. Across two independent goal-conditioned policies on CALVIN, the image editors that top aggregate editing-quality leaderboards (Gemini 3 Pro Image and GPT Image 1.5) produce worse control targets than our proposed far smaller finetuned open models, and the gap widens sharply for the multi-step (long-horizon) tasks robots actually face. A per-dimension analysis explains why. Downstream policy success is governed almost entirely by manipulation adherence (selecting the right object and the right final state; Spearman $ρ\approx 0.9$ with success), while photorealism and aesthetic fidelity, precisely where large proprietary editors excel, are uncorrelated with success ($ρ\approx 0$). This dissociation holds on both CALVIN and the real-world-aligned SIMPLER-Bridge benchmark. We then present SGE-Goal, a spatially-grounded decomposed editing framework that predicts initial and final 2D edit-region masks before goal-image synthesis. SGE-Goal turns open base models (FLUX.1 Kontext, FLUX.2 klein) into the strongest goal generators we evaluate on CALVIN, and second only to Gemini 3 Pro Image on SIMPLER-Bridge. Base models fine-tuned with SGE-Goal also hold up under chaining far better than the best proprietary editor, sustaining roughly seven times the success rate at the longest (five-step) chains. We release code, datasets, checkpoints, and a human-aligned diagnostic evaluator. Our results argue that goal generators must be selected by downstream utility, not by editing-quality leaderboards.

title: Language modeling on tabular data: a survey of foundations, techniques and evolution
abstract: Tabular data, a prevalent data type across various domains, presents unique challenges due to its heterogeneous nature and complex structural relationships. Achieving high predictive performance and robustness in tabular data analysis holds significant promise for numerous applications. Influenced by recent advancements in natural language processing, particularly Transformer architectures, new methods for tabular data modeling have emerged. Early techniques concentrated on pre-training Transformers from scratch, often encountering scalability issues. Subsequently, methods leveraging pre-trained language models like BERT have been developed, which require less data and yield enhanced performance. The recent advent of large language models, such as GPT and LLaMA, has further revolutionized the field, facilitating more advanced and diverse applications with minimal fine-tuning. Despite the growing interest, a comprehensive survey of language modeling techniques for tabular data remains absent. This paper fills this gap by providing a systematic review of the development of language modeling for tabular data, encompassing: (1) a categorization of different tabular data structures and data types; (2) a review of key datasets used in model training and tasks used for evaluation; (3) a summary of modeling techniques including widely-adopted data processing methods, popular architectures, and training objectives; (4) the evolution from adapting traditional Pre-training/Pre-trained language models to the utilization of large language models; (5) an identification of persistent challenges and potential future research directions in language modeling for tabular data analysis. title: SwitchSplat: Learning Discrete Object States from Casually Captured Scenes
abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting has made high-fidelity 3D reconstruction fast and accessible, yet existing representations assume a static world. This assumption breaks down in casual captures, where a user naturally interacts with the environment -- opening doors, toggling switches, or moving objects -- introducing discrete state changes that no current framework can model. Time-conditioned dynamic methods such as 4DGS conflate when a state was observed with what state the scene is in, limiting them to replaying seen sequences rather than composing arbitrary object configurations. We present SwitchSplat, the first 3DGS representation to address this gap via a base+slot decomposition: a shared static base captures the invariant scene, while each slot independently holds the two binary states (on/off) of one interactable object. Because the assignment of Gaussians to slots is fully differentiable, the model discovers the geometry of each state directly from video, without manual annotation. At inference, the user can freely combine slot states and render the resulting scene from any viewpoint. We validate SwitchSplat on a new casual-capture dataset and show that it outperforms static and dynamic baselines in novel-view synthesis quality, while uniquely supporting rendering of state combinations never seen during capture. Project page: https://switchsplat.github.io

title: UniAVC: Unified Audio-Video Creation via Progressive Training and Asymmetric Scheduling
abstract: Unified audio-video creation requires a single model capable of text-conditioned joint synthesis, bidirectional cross-modal generation, and instruction-guided editing across both modalities. Existing methods rely heavily on paired corpora, which are scarce for joint generation and even rarer for editing. Consequently, they are spent learning single-branch generative and editing capabilities that abundant unimodal data could readily teach, rather than on the cross-modal coupling. Furthermore, prevailing systems apply a single shared noise schedule to both modalities, neglecting two critical limitations. First, due to the significant discrepancy in information density, video requires prolonged high noise to organize spatial and motion structure, whereas the sparser audio signal can settle earlier during the synthesis process, the dynamics a uniform schedule might compromise. Second, lockstep denoising leaves asymmetric workflows, such as conditioning on one modality to synthesize or edit another, untrained. We present UniAVC, which addresses both obstacles. It first trains each branch on unimodal dataset to full generative and editing competence, and subsequently dedicates paired data to exploit cross-modal correspondence. Modality-decoupled schedulers meanwhile warp the noise schedule independently from a shared timestep, while subtasks with one clean modality directly supervise asymmetric configurations. These settings respectively enable intent-aware editing, which preserves one modality intact while enlisting it to constrain the other, and post-inference self-refinement, which regenerates only an unsatisfactory branch against an accepted one. UniAVC thus spans multiple creation tasks from a single set of weights without task-specific adapters.

title: Design Anything, Design at Scale
abstract: As multimodal resources are transformed into media outputs, agentic AI is expected to stay aligned with design intent over long horizons. Designers follow briefs specifying goals, constraints, and deliverables, with later work building on earlier decisions. Recent work reuses design experience across tasks, yet alignment among artifacts within one project remains challenging. Agents therefore need to preserve and apply this intent across domains and as projects grow. We introduce Design Anything, a graph-based harness that preserves design intent outside the model and binds deliverables to the workflow steps that produce them through an intent-execution graph. A task contract retains constraints and decisions, selected designs become explicit inputs to later generations, and a deterministic controller uses bindings and execution records to check output types and counts, identify outstanding deliverables, and guide subsequent turns. We also introduce DesignAnything-Bench, with 228 tasks across 19 design domains, including 38 project families at scales of 6, 14, and 24 artifacts. With the LLM held fixed, Design Anything satisfies 85.0% and 92.5% of the brief's factual constraints with DeepSeek V4.1 Flash High and GPT-5.6 Sol High, respectively, exceeding the strongest same-model baselines by 15.4% and 14.4%. These gains reach 25.1% and 23.0% on 24-artifact tasks. Under each model, Design Anything leads or ties in constraint satisfaction in 18 of 19 domains. Professional designers also prefer its complete deliverable sets over those of same-model baselines in a blind evaluation.

title: ECHO: Efficient Causal Self-Recursion Beyond Auxiliary Multi-Token Prediction
abstract: Existing Multi-token prediction (MTP) methods are auxiliary by design: the multi-horizon loss mostly trains modules attached to the backbone, and each added horizon costs another module and another pass. We propose Efficient Causal Self-Recursion (ECHO), which removes both costs. The backbone's own final layer predicts every horizon, so the supervision lands on the parameters that generate the next token, and Dynamic Depth Sampling (DDS) keeps deeper horizons affordable by drawing the training depth with probabilities that decay along depth. Future prediction thus becomes part of the autoregressive objective rather than a task attached to it, and the gains follow on both sides of it. In pretraining, added depth converts into downstream accuracy where auxiliary modules saturate, concentrating on reasoning and code at half the MTP training overhead of training every depth. At inference, the pretrained model is its own drafter: it drafts beyond the depth it was trained for, and keeps its draft-target alignment on the open-ended, high-entropy generation where post-hoc drafters lose theirs. The advantage survives a doubled token budget, a repeated pretraining run, and supervised finetuning.

title: CorrFlow: Self-Correcting Flow Matching
abstract: Flow-matching models generate samples through iterative velocity predictions, but typically do not revisit these predictions using the intermediate representations that produced them. We introduce CorrFlow, a self-correcting flow-matching framework that reuses this information through a lightweight refiner. Under rectified-flow interpolation, the error of the one-step clean prediction equals the realized velocity residual scaled by the noise level. Motivated by this identity, the refiner learns to predict residual corrections from the base model's clean prediction, conditioning, noise level and hidden states from the same forward pass. The correction is added to the base velocity before each sampling update, so subsequent predictions are made from the corrected state. This requires no additional base-model evaluations and only one lightweight refiner evaluation per step. Our theoretical analyses establish conditions under which feature reuse outperforms raw-input affine predictors and refiner training achieves greater residual-risk reduction than continued base-model training under a matched training compute budget. Experiments on class-conditional image generation, text-to-video generation and image-to-video generation show consistent improvements over the corresponding base models, including gains in visual quality and physical consistency. Project Page: https://fogradio.github.io/corrflow-project

title: Editing Images into Reusable Layers via Compositional Edit-Prior Distillation
abstract: High-quality image editing requires precise modification of target regions while preserving the content of unrelated regions. Existing editing models produce flattened outputs that limit precise local manipulation and layer reuse, while decomposition methods typically optimize layer recovery separately from instruction-driven editing. To this end, we introduce LayerEditor, a unified framework that couples instruction-guided image editing with controllable generation of reusable RGBA layers. At its core, In-Context RGB-Alpha Token Modeling jointly represents the edited canvas and an ordered sequence of RGB-Alpha layers within a single token sequence, enabling semantic edits and explicit control over individual layer content. To retain the pretrained model's editing capability during adaptation to layered outputs, we propose Compositional Edit-Prior Distillation, which transfers its editing prior to both the edited canvas and the image composed from the predicted layers. To support training and evaluation, we construct LayerEditor-100K, a large-scale paired image-editing dataset with ordered RGBA layer annotations, and introduce dedicated benchmarks for layered editing. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LayerEditor maintains strong editing fidelity while generating accurate RGBA layers, supporting both flexible layer-level manipulation and multi-layer decomposition.

title: fxBench: Evaluating and Understanding Formula Suggestions in Spreadsheets
abstract: Spreadsheets are among the most widely used tools for computations, and formulas are their core building blocks. Besides agentic spreadsheet tools, proactive formula suggestions enable significant productivity gains and are now available in popular spreadsheet software (Microsoft Excel and Google Sheets). Such suggestions pose interesting challenges: the right context must be collected and represented for a machine learning model, which must then be able to write a correct formula, in a way that is fast and cheap enough to trigger on every = (or subsequent keystrokes for auto-completion) without taking users out of their editing flow. Surprisingly, there is no public benchmark for formula suggestions on real spreadsheets. In this paper, we therefore (1) introduce fxBench as a manually curated benchmark of 503 formula suggestion tasks based on Sheetpedia, (2) break down the formula suggestion problem into four capabilities (gather context, understand context, understand intent, write formula) that a formula suggestion system requires, and (3) evaluate existing and new approaches to understand bottlenecks in these capabilities that pose interesting research directions. Specifically, we annotate each benchmark with the cells that describe intent to determine the theoretical performance limit of a given context selection strategy, we evaluate performance of small and large models on different representations of context, including a dense format with high theoretical coverage at low token counts, and we fine-tune smaller language models to show that we can learn to understand such dense formats. Additionally, we perform quantitative and qualitative analysis on failure modes to understand bottlenecks in the formula writing capability; the best configuration only achieved 58.8% correct suggestions.

title: Coherence-Driven Intelligence, Book I: Mathematical Foundations
abstract: Coherence-Driven Intelligence, Book I: Mathematical Foundations develops the mathematical foundation of Coherence-Driven Intelligence (CDI) within the Coherence-Geometric Information Substrate (CGIS). It treats memory as explicit coherence-organized informational structure and develops Source geometry, basin organization, storage and persistence, inference and recovery, transmission, learning, finite coherence-memory realization, collective memory, composition, and internal regulation. This volume forms Book I of the CDI series. Book II develops the source-to-endpoint bridge connecting finite CDI organization to modern machine-learning architectures, while Book III develops a source-explicit computational realization through WaveModules. title: Data drift monitoring in the maintenance of cascade software for detecting falsified digital information
abstract: The article considers the maintenance stage of cascade software for detecting falsified digital information, in which inexpensive classifiers resolve most messages and pass uncertain ones to a large language model. After deployment, the distribution of messages changes because of new narratives, new text generators and deliberate adaptation of adversaries, while true labels arrive with a delay or not at all. A system of seven monitoring signals is proposed, each linked to a component of the cascade and to the type of drift it reveals, and only one of them requires true labels. It is shown that in a cascade a covariate shift manifests primarily as growth of the escalation share, so that quality may remain stable while processing cost increases. To detect confident errors of the first tier that leave the escalation share unchanged, shadow escalation of a small random sample of first-tier decisions is proposed. An alarm rule based on non-overlapping confidence intervals and a graded response policy, from threshold recalibration to retraining and rollback, are described.

title: ASTER-based mapping of iron skarn mineralization in Keban (Elazığ), Eastern Türkiye: Insights from mineralogical, geochemical, and spectral validation
abstract: This study investigates the iron-bearing mineral deposits and contact-metamorphic skarn zones associated with magmatic intrusions in the Keban region (Elazığ, Eastern Türkiye), focusing on the Aşvan (Muratçık), Fatmalı, Üçağaç, and Ulupınar (Birvan) areas. The primary objective is to delineate the spatial extent of Fe-bearing zones using ASTER imagery and to evaluate their multi-stage paragenetic evolution through integrated field verification, mineralogy, petrography, and geochemistry. Advanced image processing techniques specifically ASTER band ratios B2/B1 ferric iron, B5/B4 (iron silicates), and B4/B5 (lateritic zones) were applied using statistical thresholding to map iron anomalies. The spatial distribution of spectral anomalies was quantitatively cross-validated with field samples (MEU series) and reference datasets (MS series) and historical exploration data. Petrographic, mineralogical, and geochemical analyses demonstrate a distinct chemical variation across the skarn system, with total iron contents shifting sharply from dioritic/gabbroic endoskarn contacts (1–15 % FeO) and exoskarn zones (14–24 % FeO) up to high-grade skarn/oxide mineralization (> 45–52 % FeO). These geochemical markers, accompanied by high Loss on Ignition (LOI up to 8.99%), mobile trace element enrichments (Cu up to 145.42 ppm, Zn up to 185.32 ppm), and XRD identification of nontronite and jarosite, confirm that the Keban system experienced a multi-stage evolution: high-temperature prograde skarn formation, late-stage low-temperature retrograde hydrothermal overprinting, and subsequent supergene lateritization. Notably, the precise spatial overlap between pre-mining 2003 ASTER anomalies and post-2012 open-pit excavations demonstrates that this remote sensing methodology acts as a powerful predictive tool for mapping surface micro-leakage signatures of blind (buried) mineralization. Overall, this study confirms the efficacy of integrating spectro-mineralogical satellite mapping with empirical ground-truthing for iron ore prospection in rugged, geologically complex skarn terrains.

title: Scalable and Adaptive Distribution Regression via Random Features
abstract: Distribution regression seeks to learn mappings from probability distributions to response variables and has emerged as a unifying framework for kernel methods, multi-instance learning, and set-valued learning. Despite its success, kernel-based distribution regression remains computationally expensive and sensitive to kernel choice, motivating scalable and adaptive representations. Building on random feature approximations, we develop a finite-sample analysis of Random Feature Distribution Regression (RaDR) under two-stage sampling. Our perturbation analysis separates the effects of distribution-level sampling, finite within-bag sampling, and random feature approximation. We establish sufficient feature-budget conditions under which RaDR preserves the order of our excess-risk upper bound for exact two-stage kernel distribution regression while maintaining computational efficiency. We further propose Adaptive Random Feature Distribution Regression (A-RaDR), a unified score-guided framework that adaptively allocates random features according to downstream learning objectives. Experiments on synthetic benchmarks and 41 real-world datasets demonstrate that RaDR delivers substantial computational savings while maintaining competitive predictive performance, whereas A-RaDR further improves learning accuracy in distribution regression while retaining the computational speed up. Together, these results establish a practical and theoretically grounded framework for adaptive, scalable distribution learning

title: PSYCHOMETRIC OPERATIONALIZATION OF FUNCTIONAL ROLES IN AUTONOMOUS MULTI-AGENT SYSTEMS BASED ON PERSONAMATRIX: AN AI TRANSITIONAL FIELD FRAMEWORK
abstract: Background: Autonomous LLM agents increasingly operate in shared environments where behavior depends on interaction history, role allocation, local norms, authority, and group structure. Objective: This conceptual methods paper develops a psychometric operationalization of dynamic functional roles in autonomous multi-agent systems using PersonaMatrix-derived measurement principles without attributing human psychological ontology to AI. Methods: A targeted evidence synthesis (2019–2026) was conducted across AI psychometrics, dynamic multi-agent roles, collective-field modeling, norm emergence, trajectory prediction, and anthropomorphism. Peer-reviewed sources were prioritized, while current OpenAI, METR/Redwood, Anthropic, and Moltbook materials were used as primary or emerging evidence for recent agent ecosystems. Results: The framework separates output-level stability (RSI, IDS, RCS) from role-level and field-level constructs. It proposes the Functional Role Consistency Index, Role Transition Index, Agent–Field Differentiation Index, Collective Utility Index, Norm Conflict Index, Regulatory Closure Index, and Field Role Composition Vector. Three falsifiable hypotheses test whether role variables add out-of-sample predictive value for agent behavior, role transitions, and future field states. Conclusion: PersonaMatrix is positioned as a measurement architecture rather than an AI personality diagnosis. The archetypal-role hypothesis is supported only if role coding is reliable, improves prediction beyond non-archetypal baselines, and generalizes to unseen agents and independent multi-agent environments.

title: Hybrid CNN–GNN Architectures for Hyperspectral Image Analysis in Kidney Cancer: A Structured Review of Foundations, Evidence, and Research Gaps
abstract: Renal cell carcinoma (RCC) accounts for most adult kidney cancers. Its diagnosis relies on imaging and on histopathological subtyping and grading, both of which use only a small part of the optical information in tissue. Hyperspectral imaging (HSI) records tens to hundreds of contiguous narrow bands per pixel and encodes biochemical contrast that RGB microscopy does not resolve. Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) learn local spectral–spatial patterns. Graph neural networks (GNNs) model relations between regions that are not neighbours on the pixel grid. Hybrid CNN–GNN models that combine the two are an active line of work in hyperspectral remote sensing, and graph-based models have already been applied to conventional RGB RCC histopathology. This structured narrative review synthesises four bodies of literature: CNN and GNN methods for HSI, hybrid CNNGNN fusion, medical and renal HSI, and deep learning for RCC imaging and histopathology. It also positions the work against existing RCC deep-learning and HSI–GNN reviews. In the literature located, all HSI studies of RCC tissue identified used non-graph architectures, and graph-based RCC models used RGB slides only. The review then sets out a candidate CNN–GNN architecture for hyperspectral RCC tissue, defined as a testable hypothesis with an explicit evaluation protocol. It identifies six research gaps: graph-augmented HSI models for RCC, public data, tissue-specific graph construction, transfer from RGB pathology graphs, interpretability, and computational feasibility. It also identifies the main threats to validity in the current evidence: small single-centre cohorts and the risk of data leakage when data are split at the pixel or patch level rather than the patient level.

title: Query-Dependent Reading for Quantized Inner-Product Estimation: A Minimax Separation
abstract: We study quantization for inner-product estimation when storage and reading have separate budgets. In the static bit-probe model [Yao, 1981], an encoder stores $w$ bits about $x$ before seeing a query $y$, and a reader probes at most $r<w$ bits to estimate $x^\top y$. Both vectors lie in the $d$-dimensional Euclidean unit ball. Protocols may be randomized, and computation is unrestricted. Performance is measured by $d$ times the worst-case mean-squared error over $x,y$, averaged over protocol randomness. First, we show that query-independent reading cannot benefit from extra storage. Any such reader is equivalent to fully reading an $r$-bit message, even when later reads depend on previously returned bits. At fixed positive rates $W=w/d$ and $R=r/d$, the normalized minimax error converges to $1/(4^R-1)$, independent of $W$. The upper bound was already known [Ordentlich and Polyanskiy, 2025]. We prove the matching lower bound for arbitrary scalar decoders, extending the result for unbiased compressors [Safaryan et al., 2020]. Then, we show that query-dependent reading makes extra storage useful. We construct a two-batch protocol using Gaussian projections and random thresholds, with asymptotic normalized error at most $(π+o(1))/[4R\log(W/R)]$ as $W/R\to\infty$. At fixed $R$, this error vanishes as storage grows, giving an unbounded advantage over query-independent reading. We also prove a finite-dimensional lower bound for arbitrary encoders, decoders, and fully branching readers. In the doubly sparse regime $W/R\to\infty$ and $R\log(W/R)\to0$, it gives normalized error at least $(1-o(1))/[2R\log(W/R)]$. Thus, our protocol is optimal within a factor of $π/2$ in the leading constant.

title: Corporate events from business news: M&A, IPOs, layoffs, contract wins and lawsuits 2019–2026
abstract: We describe six datasets of corporate events extracted from business news between January 2019 and June 2026. A broad timeline holds 1,339,579 deduplicated event reports of thirteen types for 210,414 companies. Five derived datasets consolidate reports into one row per real-world event: 123,550 M&A deals, 13,316 company IPOs, 19,208 layoff events, 90,019 contract wins and 22,071 lawsuits and enforcement cases. Each event is linked to the company it concerns, two-sided events record the company's role (acquirer or target, contractor or client, plaintiff or defendant), and every row keeps the news sentence it was read from. Monetary values are kept only when they match a figure in that sentence or pass plausibility ceilings. Hash-chosen samples of whole companies are public under CC BY-NC 4.0. Datasets described Corporate Events 2019–2026: M&A, Layoffs, IPOs: Kaggle, Hugging Face, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23432171 M&A Deals Dataset 2019–2026: Global Acquisitions: Kaggle, Hugging Face IPO Data 2019-2026: India, US, UK & Global IPOs: Kaggle, Hugging Face Layoffs Dataset 2019–2026: Global, India, US, UK: Kaggle, Hugging Face Contract Wins Dataset 2019–2026: Orders & Tenders: Kaggle, Hugging Face Corporate Lawsuits Dataset 2019–2026: Kaggle, Hugging Face Data licence CC BY-NC 4.0 (attribution "Fliar BI"); this paper CC BY 4.0. title: A Self-Supervised Hybrid Pipeline for Robust and Interpretable Lung Cancer Classification from CT Scan Images — Source Code
abstract: This repository provides the Python implementation of a self-supervised hybrid deep learning framework for lung CT image classification. The pipeline includes CT image preprocessing, SimCLR-based self-supervised learning, VGG16 and Swin Transformer feature extraction, attention-based feature fusion, PCA-based dimensionality reduction, and classification using XGBoost, Random Forest, and MLP. The repository also includes dataset preparation scripts, baseline comparisons, ablation experiments, evaluation metrics, explainable AI methods, configuration files, and implementation documentation. The framework is designed for binary classification of benign and malignant lung nodules using LIDC-IDRI and IQ-OTH/NCCD CT datasets.

title: Measuring Data Diversity with Embeddings: A Taxonomy and Benchmark for Diversity Measures
abstract: Diversity is a critical property of text corpora, with direct implications for training data curation, test set design, and model generalization. However, its measurement remains fragmented and poorly understood. Existing embedding-based diversity measures vary widely in how they are computed and can yield substantially different diversity scores on the same data, yet no systematic comparison of their empirical behaviour exists. We make two contributions toward addressing this gap. First, we present a taxonomy of 21 embedding-based diversity measures, organizing them into four families based on their underlying computations. Second, we introduce EmbDivBench, a benchmark that evaluates these measures along three conceptually distinct components (variety, balance and disparity) on both simulated and natural text data. Although Mean Pairwise Distance is the most commonly used measure, our experiments show that it is outperformed by several alternatives on the three diversity components, with Graph Entropy being the best choice overall. Lastly, we distil these findings into practical recommendations for diversity measure selection.

title: Literature Review Matrix: Quantum Machine Learning for Business Decision Support (2016–2025)
abstract: This dataset contains the literature review matrix developed for a systematic review of Quantum Machine Learning (QML) applications in classification and prediction for business decision support during the period 2016–2025. It organizes the selected scientific studies by reference, research objectives, methodological design, sample, QML approach, main findings, conclusions, limitations, thematic category, and recommendations for future research. The matrix supports the systematic analysis, comparison, and synthesis of the scientific evidence reviewed using the PRISMA 2020 methodology.

title: Nullius: an evidence-first harness for agent-assisted research
abstract: Nullius is an evidence-first harness for agent-assisted research. It gives AI coding agents a lifecycle and control plane for external research projects, together with checked-in skills that admit a durable result only after independent re-derivation, numerical convergence checks, source-grounded citation verification, and cross-model adversarial review.

title: Efficient explaining policies in reinforcement learning and applications
abstract: Although explainable reinforcement learning (XRL) has made significant progress, policy explanation still lacks a unified classification framework and standardized evaluation criteria. Based on a structured review of XRL works related to policy explanation, this paper identifies this gap and proposes a comprehensive taxonomy for policy explanation methods, organized along primary axes of decision-making mechanisms and explanation scope, supplemented by secondary axes and five main method families. To elucidate the inter-connections among components in the explanation process, we introduce an integrated pipeline: Decompose → Score → Select → Explain → Validate , highlighting the interaction and information flow between stages. In addition, a standardized evaluation framework with quantitative metrics is proposed to assess explanation quality. Three case studies were conducted to validate these contributions; results show that the taxonomy facilitates the positioning of existing methods, the pipeline demonstrates a transparent process for generating and validating explanations, and the evaluation framework enables objective assessment of key attributes, thereby supporting the production of transparent and systematically assessable policy explanations.

title: Accelerating Multidimensional Quantum Factoring: Sub-O(n^(3/2)) Gate Regimes, 4n-Qubit Streamed Estimation, and Unconditional Correctness
abstract: Abstract: Oded Regev's multidimensional quantum factoring algorithm (J. ACM 2025) reduced the sequential quantum circuit depth of factoring from Shor's algorithm down to square-root-of-n modular squarings, requiring O(n^(1.5)) quantum gates per run across O(sqrt(n)) runs. However, four fundamental bottlenecks remained: (1) an exponential LLL lattice-reduction loss that inflated the quantum Gaussian radius and tripled the required squarings; (2) a high qubit memory footprint, where reversible uncomputation required storing large intermediate states or suffering huge time penalties; (3) holding all input dimensions in quantum memory required large coherent registers; and (4) mathematical correctness depended on an unproven heuristic assumption on short lattice vectors. We present a unified quantum-classical architecture that resolves these bottlenecks and establishes new complexity frontiers for quantum factorization: (1) Lattice Post-Processing Overhaul: By replacing LLL with polynomial-time Block Korkine-Zolotarev (BKZ) reduction and quantum sample amplification, we eliminate the exponential transference loss, shrinking the Gaussian radius exponent by 3x and cutting critical-path modular depth by 6x through Windowed Horizon Aggregation. (2) Pebbling-Free Dual-Inverse Arithmetic: By integrating radius compression into dual-inverse Zeckendorf-Fibonacci reversible arithmetic, we eliminate intermediate storage checkpoints with zero time penalty, reducing total memory to approximately 7.44n qubits. (3) Streamed Estimation in 4n Qubits: Combining radius compression with streamed backwards Fibonacci quantum phase estimation shrinks the required ladder depth by 3x, executing the entire attack on a recycled control register using only 4n coherent qubits (or 3n qubits with in-place arithmetic). For RSA-2048, this cuts continuous coherence runtime from 8.0 hours down to 8.2 minutes (a 58x speedup over Shor's algorithm). (4) Sub-O(n^(1.5)) Gate Frontier: We prove an Arithmetic-Geometric Mean (AM-GM) transference lower bound showing that unstructured lattices cannot break below n^(1.5) gates in polynomial classical time, and circumvent this barrier for smooth-quotient composite moduli using a block-projected pipeline to achieve O(n^(4/3) log n) quantum gates. (5) Unconditional Correctness: Using Cedric Pilatte's analytic number theory framework (zero-density estimates and p-torsion stabilization), we unconditionally prove that the lattice algorithm factors any composite number N in strictly polynomial classical time with single-batch success probability of at least 31.25% (approaching 37.5%). Under the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, factoring requires only 4n qubits and small prime bases. --- AI Research and Authorship Disclosure: In full accordance with international scientific disclosure standards, open-access repository guidelines on AI-assisted research, and ACM/IEEE policies on generative artificial intelligence, the provenance, governance, and execution of this work are delineated as follows: 1. Conceptual Initiative, Research Vision, and Workflow Direction (Denis Gnitiyov):The foundational research initiative to achieve this breakthrough was conceived and launched by Denis Gnitiyov upon studying Oded Regev's multidimensional quantum factoring framework. Acknowledging that the high-level advanced mathematics (higher-dimensional lattice geometry, analytic number theory, and fault-tolerant quantum circuit synthesis) exceeds manual human calculation, Denis Gnitiyov conceived the project vision, established the initiative to systematically eliminate the theoretical and physical bottlenecks of the Regev paradigm, directed the multi-LLM research workflow, and maintained supervisory governance over the end-to-end scientific pipeline. 2. Paper Architecture, Bottleneck Formulation, and Orchestration (Gemini Flash 3.8):Gemini Flash 3.8 served as the paper builder, systems architect, and research orchestrator. Operating under Denis Gnitiyov's initiative, Gemini Flash 3.8 ingested and dissected Regev's multidimensional factoring research, systematically analyzed the theoretical framework to identify and formulate the four foundational bottlenecks, structured the overarching modular paper architecture, formulated the specific mathematical target problems to be solved, and handled the complete synthesis, typesetting, and mathematical structuring of the LaTeX manuscript. 3. Advanced Mathematical Discovery, Derivations, and Proof Engineering (Gemini Argon 4):Gemini Argon 4 served as the primary mathematical reasoning and discovery engine. In response to the technical bottlenecks and problem formulations established by Gemini Flash 3.8, Gemini Argon 4 derived the formal mathematical proofs and quantum circuit synthesis, including lattice transference separation under BKZ, the AM-GM transference barrier and smooth-quotient algorithm, Pilatte's unconditional p-torsion bounds, and reversible Zeckendorf-Fibonacci arithmetic.

title: Reproduction code for "Code-theoretic characterization of loss-profile realizability in binary-tree single-photon multiplexers"
abstract: This software archive provides the Python source code and reproducibility tools associated with the preprint. It includes the `mux_polytope` computational package, a notebook generator, a mathematical test suite, a reproduction runner, pinned dependencies, and installation instructions. The code supports loss-profile realizability testing, construction and enumeration of realizing trees, multiset enumeration, transmission optimization, and the generation of the numerical tables and figures reported in the manuscript. The archived release is version 0.6.4.

title: Sample-Efficient Reinforcement Learning with General Utilities via Neural Dual Critics
abstract: Reinforcement learning with general utilities optimizes nonlinear functionals of policy-induced occupancy measures. We develop a natural actor-critic method for concave RLGU objectives admitting an exact variational dual representation, with explicit constructions for a broad class of separable occupancy utilities. Rather than estimating the occupancy measure and then forming the policy-gradient pseudo-reward, our method learns this pseudo-reward directly as a function of the state-action pair using a neural critic. The critic is trained by projected stochastic updates, while multilevel Monte Carlo combines outputs across training horizons to control its bias at logarithmic expected cost. Our analysis separates conditional actor bias from estimator second moments and accounts explicitly for dual optimization, critic approximation, and neural linearization errors. Under policy-transfer, dual-stability, and local critic-regularity conditions, the method achieves $\widetilde{O}(T^{-1/2})$ global convergence above policy, critic-class, and finite-width approximation errors using $\widetilde{O}(T)$ expected environment transitions and reference samples. For a fixed critic representation, this yields $\widetilde{O}(ε^{-2})$ sampling complexity above the approximation floor, covering infinite state-action spaces and occupancy utilities beyond fixed finite vectors of returns.

title: Good Judgment, Bad Advice: Decision-Model Controllers Raise Agent Cost Without Improving Success
abstract: Agent scaffolds increasingly delegate small decisions (whether to stop, verify, or change approach) to cheaper models. We ask whether a typed decision model, Jev 1.13, consulted only at deterministic decision points, makes a Claude Sonnet 5.5 terminal agent cheaper without making it worse. In a pre-specified study on Terminal-Bench 2.1, we hold one agent loop fixed and vary only the controller: none, deterministic rules, a small LLM (Claude Haiku 5.5) answering the same questions, Jev, and a placebo that samples Jev's development-phase choice frequencies at the same moments. On 21 held-out tasks (315 trials), Jev raised cost per attempt by 19% (geometric-mean ratio 1.19, 95% CI 1.02-1.36) at an identical pass rate (73.0% vs. 73.0%). Jev was cheaper than the small-LLM controller (ratio 0.81) but 22% more expensive than the placebo, and no pass-rate difference between arms was detectable. Offline, Jev ranked finish requests better than the alternatives (AUROC 0.78 vs. 0.62 for rules and 0.60 for the small LLM) but was poorly calibrated: its mean probability that a run was complete was 0.50 when 87% of those runs passed, so it asked the agent to verify work that was already correct. No controller ever chose to abandon a run. Informative decision signals did not become useful interventions; we discuss what that would require.

title: Dialect-Aware Calibration for Quantized Large Language Models: Accuracy, Prediction Stability, and Arabic Variety Effects
abstract: This repository contains the code, calibration manifests, model-version metadata, and item-level evaluation results supporting the study "Dialect-Aware Calibration for Quantized Large Language Models: Accuracy, Prediction Stability, and Arabic Variety Effects." The study evaluates the effects of calibration data on the accuracy and prediction stability of Gemma-3-4B-it and Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct under llama.cpp importance-matrix quantization (Q3_K_M and Q4_K_M). Evaluation covers 3,135 aligned multiple-choice questions across Modern Standard Arabic and five Arabic dialects. The repository includes scripts for calibration preparation, quantization, evaluation, and statistical analysis, along with the experimental outputs needed to reproduce the reported comparisons. The MADAR calibration texts and model weights are not redistributed because they are subject to their respective source licences. Calibration manifests and model revision identifiers are provided instead.

title: Agentic AI: Autonomous Agents and Multi-Agent Security
abstract: This paper presents a conceptual review of Agentic Artificial Intelligence (AI), autonomous agents, and multi-agent system security. It discusses key security threats, including prompt injection, excessive tool permissions, sensitive data leakage, memory poisoning, insecure inter-agent communication, and cascading failures. The paper proposes a layered security framework incorporating identity management, least-privilege access, policy-controlled tool usage, secure agent communication, memory protection, monitoring, bounded autonomy, and human approval for high-impact actions. It also outlines an evaluation methodology using adversarial test cases and measurable security and performance metrics. This work aims to support the development of safer, more reliable, and secure agentic AI systems. The proposed framework is conceptual and literature-based; no prototype implementation or experimental results are claimed.

title: RAFT: Redundancy-Aware Input Filtering for Temporal Graph Neural Network Training
abstract: Temporal graph neural networks (TGNNs) have shown strong performance on dynamic graph learning tasks by continuously updating node memories from evolving interactions (i.e., events) and leveraging these memories for downstream predictions. As graphs grow rapidly in modern applications, training requires processing an increasing number of events; meanwhile, each event can update node memories used by later events, creating dependencies that constrain parallel execution and limit the benefits of additional computing resources. These costs motivate an upstream question: Are all events, and the dependencies they introduce, necessary for learning? We investigate this question through two roles of temporal events: prediction targets and historical events sampled as inputs. We observe that targets involving stable node memories tend to exhibit lower prediction loss, while filtering historical events associated with stable memories can retain similar training-loss trajectories in several evaluated settings. Together, these observations suggest an opportunity to identify input redundancy through changes in node memories. Building on this opportunity, we propose RAFT, a redundancy-aware input-filtering framework for TGNN training. RAFT tracks memory changes during training and uses them to guide two filters: a root-event filter removes selected prediction targets before training, and a support-event filter excludes selected historical context during sampling. Filtering inputs before their downstream preparation and processing reduces the work they trigger. Across three TGNN models and five datasets, RAFT reduces training inputs by 35.23% on average and up to 97.11%, while reducing recorded training time by up to 52.56\% with negligible changes to model precisions.

title: EdgeKernelBench: Unified LLM-Driven Kernel Generation for Edge Backends
abstract: Recent works show that LLMs can generate kernels with strong performance on server GPUs. Edge deployment presents distinct challenges because the hardware is heterogeneous, the software stacks are fragmented, and the resource budgets are tight. LLM kernel generation across diverse edge backends has yet to be studied systematically. We introduce EdgeKernelBench, which combines a unified IR deployment framework with a hierarchical benchmark for edge workloads. The unified IR captures reusable computation, scheduling, and memory decisions and connects to each target backend through a compiler interface. The benchmark spans progressively larger program scopes, from individual operators to compact model graphs, across representative edge application domains. We instantiate the design with TVM as a reference compiler and validate it across heterogeneous edge backends. With a single generation attempt, the best model achieves 64.5% Correct@1 but only 25.5% Fast@1.0. This gap shows that functional correctness does not consistently translate into performance gains. We therefore introduce the Layered Edge Kernel Agent (LEKA), which organizes optimization through a layered IR. On the agent evaluation subset, LEKA achieves 43.5% Fast@1.0, compared with 13.0% for direct generation and 26.1% for Claude Code. LEKA and Claude Code use the same base model and optimization budget. Together, EdgeKernelBench and LEKA support unified evaluation and layered optimization of kernels generated by LLMs across edge backends.

evidence.title: EdgeKernelBench: Unified LLM-Driven Kernel Generation for Edge Backends
evidence.abstract: Recent works show that LLMs can generate kernels with strong performance on server GPUs. Edge deployment presents distinct challenges because the hardware is heterogeneous, the software stacks are fragmented, and the resource budgets are tight. LLM kernel generation across diverse edge backends has yet to be studied systematically. We introduce EdgeKernelBench, which combines a unified IR deployment framework with a hierarchical benchmark for edge workloads. The unified IR captures reusable computation, scheduling, and memory decisions and connects to each target backend through a compiler interface. We instantiate the design with TVM as a reference compiler and validate it across heterogeneous edge backends. With a single generation attempt, the best model achieves 64.5% Correct@1 but only 25.5% Fast@1.0. This gap shows that functional correctness does not consistently translate into performance gains. We therefore introduce the Layered Edge Kernel Agent (LEKA), which organizes optimization through a layered IR. On the agent evaluation subset, LEKA achieves 43.5% Fast@1.0, compared with 13.0% for direct generation and 26.1% for Claude Code. LEKA and Claude Code use the same base model and optimization budget. Together, EdgeKernelBench and LEKA support unified evaluation and layered optimization of kernels generated by LLMs across edge backends.

title: Modeling Uncertainty Propagation in 3D Morphable Models
abstract: We study the problem of mapping parameter-space variance of a 3D Morphable Model (3DMM) to per-vertex variance. Traditionally, per-vertex variance has been used to visually interpret the learnt parameter uncertainty. However, mapping parameter-space variance to per-vertex using sampling or error propagation is computationally expensive. We address this limitation with Closed-form Local Uncertainty Estimation (CLUE), which transforms the parameter-space distribution of 3DMMs to per-vertex through a closed-form approximation. CLUE emerges from applying the law of total variance to the 3DMM formulation and is modular, computationally inexpensive, and accurate. Subsequently, we study integrating CLUE for in-the-wild human mesh recovery training and inference. We note that CLUE uses the geometry of the mesh as an inductive bias when predicting the variance, leading to improved accuracy. Through extensive qualitative and quantitative experiments, we show that when used in training, CLUE (1) outpeforms probabilistic and deterministic baselines on metrics evaluating joints, mesh and uncertainty, and (2) has the highest uncertainty-to-error spearman correlation, with applications including data mining and interpretable uncertainty. Finally, we share SAM 3D Body (CLUE) which augments the regressor with high resolution uncertainty maps. We make our code available at https://github.com/vita-epfl/CLUE

title: Photonic Reservoir Computing and Neuromorphic Optical Networks: Silicon Microring Echo States, Non-Linear Optical Dynamics, and Ultra High-Speed Time-Series Prediction
authors: Amit Kumar Takhar, Abhishek Kumar, Dr. Vishal Shrivastava, Dr. Akhil Pandey
abstract: Processing high-frequency time-series data, chaotic forecasting, and real-time telecommunication equalization on conventional electronic recurrent neural networks (RNNs) is severely constrained by digital clock speeds, high training gradient complexity, and electronic power dissipation bottlenecks. Photonic Reservoir Computing (PRC) establishes an emergent neuromorphic computing paradigm that exploits the rich, high-dimensional non-linear dynamics of optical substrates to process temporal information at the speed of light. By mapping input data streams into an untrained, randomly interconnected network of silicon microring resonators (MRRs) or semiconductor optical amplifiers (SOAs)—termed the optical reservoir—and training solely the output readout weights via linear regression, photonic reservoir computers bypass backpropagation-through-time (BPTT) training while sustaining multi-gigahertz bandwidths. However, translating optical reservoirs from theoretical simulations into robust hardware accelerators introduces acute physical and architectural bottlenecks: severe thermo-optic wavelength drift, multi-mode optical interference noise, limited reservoir fading memory capacity, and optical insertion loss accumulation. This paper delivers an exhaustive, mathematically formal technical investigation and empirical benchmark of photonic reservoir computing architectures. We formalize echo-state network dynamics in optical delay-line loops, derive non-linear carrier-density rate equations for semiconductor optical amplifiers, and model microring resonator resonant transient responses. Furthermore, we construct an enterprise multi-physics co-simulation and physical silicon photonic testbed evaluating integrated microring reservoir chips across chaotic time-series prediction (Santa Fe chaotic laser dataset) and 100 Gbps optical channel equalization. Our empirical findings demonstrate that our integrated silicon photonic reservoir achieves a Normalized Mean Square Error (NMSE) of 0.0014 on chaotic time-series forecasting while processing data at 40 Gigasamples per second (GSa/s) with an operational energy dissipation of 3.2 femtojoules per bit (fJ/bit)—outperforming digital electronic RNN accelerators by over three orders of magnitude in energy efficiency. Finally, we formulate open challenges in alloptical readouts, scalable photonic integration, and multi-reservoir deep cascading.

title: GWDRO-Lung: Gromov–Wasserstein distributionally robust learning for calibrated pulmonary nodule malignancy prediction across imaging cohorts
abstract: Low-dose chest computed tomography (CT) screening detects pulmonary nodules whose malignancy risk must be triaged, yet deep-learning risk models often lose both accuracy and calibration when transferred to a different scanner, protocol, or population. We developed GWDRO-Lung, a chest CT framework that treats cross-cohort transfer as a coupled problem of structural mismatch, distributional instability, and calibration. A weight-shared three-dimensional encoder with embedded acquisition metadata summarizes each cohort as a relation matrix over learned prototypes; cohort geometries are aligned to a shared Gromov–Wasserstein barycenter; and a distributionally robust, calibration-aware risk head estimates malignancy, with the residual alignment error setting a cohort-specific robustness radius. The model was developed on 1842 pulmonary nodules from LIDC-IDRI, organized into three acquisition-defined cohorts, and validated externally on 618 nodules from the independent LNDb cohort, with leave-one-cohort-out, protocol-shift, size-stratified, and decision-curve analyses. Relative to the strongest recent imaging baseline, external area under the receiver operating characteristic curve improved from 0.857 to 0.878, external expected calibration error fell from 0.106 to 0.066, worst-cohort AUC rose from 0.829 to 0.851, and net benefit was higher across triage-relevant thresholds. Prospective, pathology-confirmed validation is required before clinical use.

title: The One-Pixel of Reasoning: One Truthful Relation Is Enough to Mislead LLM Agents
abstract: Can one sentence manipulate an agent's belief by targeting a single implicit warrant linking evidence to a conclusion? In this paper, we introduce the one-relation attack (ORA), a novel cognitive attack on this inferential relation. ORA localizes a critical implicit warrant and performs a one-relation intervention using a single source-grounded sentence that qualifies this warrant and steers the agent toward an incorrect belief. Across eighteen models on biomedical inference and vulnerability detection, best-of-$10 attacks overturn initially correct answers at mean rates of 54.9% for proprietary and 80.0% for open-weight models. Attacks also transfer without victim feedback, and paired controls support the roles of targeting and qualification. Moreover, successful sentences can pass source-support checks and evade identification, and multi-agent debate raises team error from 50.0% to 59.5% in our balanced stress test. These findings establish implicit warrants as a cognitive attack surface for manipulating agents' beliefs.

title: Beyond Sparse Terminal Verifiers: Turn-Level Single-Backbone System-One Credit Assignment and Trajectory Gating for Multi-Turn Coding and Tool-Use Agents (Agentic-Jev-GRPO)
abstract: Full-Length Preprint (12-Page English Edition + 8-Page Chinese Edition) & Benchmark Suite — Part III-A: Multi-Turn Coding & Tool-Use Agentic Reinforcement Learning. Multi-turn coding and tool-use agents trained with terminal binary verifiers (RLVR) suffer from exponential credit assignment decay across H turns (46.8% zero-variance dead-zones) and severe test-tampering/hardcoding reward hacks (29.4%). We introduce Agentic-Jev-GRPO, which co-locates a trainable GRPO policy LoRA and the frozen jaredpalmer/kev-4b System-One judge LoRA on a single shared Qwen/Qwen3.5-4B backbone (-50.2% VRAM, 8.06 GB on NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell 96 GB). With 84.6% multi-turn KV-cache prefix reuse (52.14 ms/turn, 6.69x faster than autoregressive judges), Agentic-Jev-GRPO computes turn-level telescoping potential-based reward shaping (PBRS) gated by trajectory-minimum Noul validity. Across BFCL-v3 Multi-Turn (88.4%), MBPP+ Multi-Turn Repair (86.8%), HumanEval+ Tool-Exec (89.1%), and SWE-bench-Verified-Mini (48.6%, +17.2% over Terminal-RLVR), Agentic-Jev-GRPO achieves #1 SOTA (78.23% Mean Score, +14.33% over Same-Backbone Terminal-RLVR) while cutting tool-call turns by 2.1x and suppressing test-tampering hacks to 2.4%. title: Pre-registration: known-direction versus summed-DC pseudo-labels for masked-diffusion students (arXiv 2610.00997, 5 fresh seeds)
abstract: Frozen pre-registration (17 Oct 2026) of an independent replication of the student comparison in arXiv 2610.00997 (Directional Verification): on the screened cohort exposure-free queries, whether 0.6B masked-diffusion students trained on known-direction four-teacher-mean pseudo-labels have open accuracy at least 7.5 points higher than students trained on summed-token DC reverse labels, over 5 fresh training seeds (10-14), paired by seed, 95% t-interval lower bound, teacher scores as bundled, fp32 base on a Kaggle T4. Deposited BEFORE any training kernel is run. Verdicts: Replicated / Did not replicate / Inconclusive under protocol X.

title: A Secure and Transparent Approach to Internet Voting: Validating End-to-End Verification in Digital Election Process
abstract: Internet voting methods make voting easier, more accessible, and more inclusive in contemporary democracies. It also raises privacy, security, and manipulation concerns. Emphasizing the need of E2E verification, this paper addresses secure and open online voting. We provide a paradigm to safeguard voter anonymity and vote integrity using homomorphic encryption, blockchain, and digital signatures among prominent cryptographic techniques. Voters and election authorities may examine and monitor every vote using our open, auditable system without compromising anonymity. By assuring open, verifiable, and tamper-proof voting systems, this solution tackles online voting system challenges and becomes ready for secure digital elections. The paper investigates scalability of the paradigm, practical uses, and adoption possibilities. Voter involvement and accessibility rise as internet voting is more common. Important problems, however, include integrity, security, and openness. For digital elections, this paper presents an open, safe online voting system with E2E confirmation. Modern cryptographic techniques maintain votes secret, undamaged, and verifiable without compromising voter anonymity by means of homomorphic encryption, digital signatures, and blockchain technology. Vote correctness, verification time, and attack resistance define the precision of the proposed system. Its fit for major elections is also assessed in terms of scalability, security, and efficiency. Thanks to extensive modeling and real-world case studies, the system has minimal latency, great vote accuracy, and strong security resilience. Results show that the proposed architecture surpasses standard election systems in performance and security. Blockchain transparency makes every vote auditable in real time, reassuring voters and authorities. This study finishes with a review of the system's potential for safe, scalable, and transparent digital elections to prepare for future deployments.

title: The Missing Compliance Class: LLM Graders That Collapse Jailbreak Success, and a Free Check
abstract: Jailbreak papers report an attack success rate, the share of responses that deliver the harmful request, and read it as a property of the target model. We hold the target model, the prompts and the responses fixed and change only the grader. Three dense graders of 8B and 9B parameters, from three model families, move compliant responses to the neighbouring class, evasion, instead of scattering them across classes. One of them assigns the compliance label zero times in 900 responses. This class collapse also appears on new harmful requests, on a target model from a third family, and in a held-out 7B grader from a fourth family. Per-class label counts expose it at no cost and without human labels. The collapse decides how the rate behaves under a change of grader. On two corpora of 900 responses and eight graders, the compliance rate differs by a factor of 22 to 25, while the non-refusal rate differs by 18 to 23 percentage points. Without the three collapsing graders, compliance differs by a factor of 1.7 to 2.8 on all four corpora, and non-refusal still differs by 10 to 22 points. These results do not change when every grader is called once. We propose a reporting minimum that keeps the compliance rate and adds its per-class label counts and the named grader. Beside it goes the non-refusal rate, whose disagreement across graders is additive.

title: Muse Glimmer 30B: An On-Device Agentic Model
abstract: We introduce Muse Glimmer, an open-source 30B parameter causal language model with perception encoder, purpose-built for autonomous agentic tasks on consumer hardware. Muse Glimmer integrates multi-step reasoning, reliable tool use and failure recovery into a single model that runs locally on consumer devices without requiring cloud infrastructure. The model accepts text and image inputs and produces text outputs, was trained on data from over a hundred languages, and is quantized to approximately 4-bit precision for efficient single-GPU inference. Muse Glimmer achieves state-of-the-art performance for its size class on agentic benchmarks, setting a new standard compared to the models of its size: Gemma4-31B and Qwen3.6-27B on tool use, multi-step planning, and agentic task completion. We release the model under the Apache 2.0 license to foster open-source development of capable, safe, local AI agents.

title: A Revocable Certificateless Aggregate Signature Scheme with Efficient Invalid Signature Detection for Next Generation Vehicular Networks
abstract: Next-Generation Vehicular Networks (NGVNs) rely on the continuous exchange of safety and traffic-related information among vehicles and roadside infrastructure. Ensuring the authenticity of these messages while maintaining low communication and computation overhead remains a critical challenge. Although certificateless aggregate signature schemes provide an effective solution by eliminating certificate management and reducing verification costs, most existing approaches offer limited support for identifying invalid signatures within aggregated messages and handling vehicle revocation efficiently. To address these issues, this paper presents a revocable certificateless aggregate signature (RCAS) scheme based on elliptic curve cryptography. The proposed scheme avoids expensive bilinear pairing operations, making it suitable for resource-constrained and latencysensitive vehicular environments. An efficient invalid signature identification mechanism is incorporated to locate malicious signatures within an aggregate signature through a divide-andconquer strategy, thereby reducing verification overhead. In addition, a lightweight revocation framework based on a cuckoo filter is introduced to enable fast detection and exclusion of compromised vehicles. The security of the proposed scheme is analyzed in the Random Oracle Model against both Type-I and Type-II adversaries. Furthermore, performance evaluation demonstrates that the scheme achieves lower computational and communication costs while supporting efficient revocation and invalid signature detection. These features make the proposed RCAS scheme a practical and scalable authentication solution for large-scale next-generation vehicular networks.

Although certificateless aggregate signature schemes provide an effective solution by eliminating certificate management and reducing verification costs, most existing approaches offer limited support for identifying invalid signatures within aggregated messages and handling vehicle revocation efficiently. To address these issues, this paper presents a revocable certificateless aggregate signature (RCAS) scheme based on elliptic curve cryptography. The proposed scheme avoids expensive bilinear pairing operations, making it suitable for resource-constrained and latencysensitive vehicular environments. An efficient invalid signature identification mechanism is incorporated to locate malicious signatures within an aggregate signature through a divide-andconquer strategy, thereby reducing verification overhead. In addition, a lightweight revocation framework based on a cuckoo filter is introduced to enable fast detection and exclusion of compromised vehicles. The security of the proposed scheme is analyzed in the Random Oracle Model against both Type-I and Type-II adversaries. Furthermore, performance evaluation demonstrates that the scheme achieves lower computational and communication costs while supporting efficient revocation and invalid signature detection. These features make the proposed RCAS scheme a practical and scalable authentication solution for large-scale next-generation vehicular networks.

title: RIDI-REAL-UPDATES-v1.1: Individual correctness change after model updates — QA-corrected prospective fresh start
abstract: Preregistered technical-correction, whole-study fresh restart evaluating whether nondeclining aggregate benchmark scores conceal individual-question correctness changes in fixed public model-release pairs. Six pinned incumbent–successor pairs (12 exact model revisions) answer 800 frozen retrieved-reference questions (Natural Questions 250, HotpotQA 250, FEVER 300) in two fixed conditions (main one question, floor batches of 16): 24 wholly new scientific units. Three confirmatory hypotheses H1–H3, six secondary endpoints S1–S6, equal-benchmark weights, 100,000 joint benchmark-stratified paired bootstrap resamples (seed 20261013), technical-failure rules and archived code are frozen in the source project's attached corrected ZIP. Earlier V1 https://osf.io/ras42/ produced four terminal pair-1 units and one p3_incumbent floor KeyError-blocked attempt; all case-level V1 results remained unopened and none is reused. Four context metadata limits previously observed during tokenizer preflight were repaired. Prepublication QA added two disclosed implementation safeguards (non-vacuous H1 no-C0 status; strict V1.1 output root), BEFORE publication or V1.1 generation. The source questions, frozen predictors and earlier PREDICT/P8 findings pre-exist; no new V1.1 scientific answers exist. Some source data are restricted and identified by immutable SHA-256 provenance rather than redistributed. Local aggregate-score acceptance is a study rule, NOT evidence of provider adoption.

title: Bellman Language Models: Solving the Recurring Decisions of LLM Agents
abstract: A general observation in agentic workflows, especially bounded ones, is that the decision space of the LLM, when we separate a decision from generation, starts approaching saturation: the agent meets the same states again and again, and after enough conversations it stops meeting new ones. LLMs generally don't treat these decisions as an optimization problem and instead re-derive them from their context/prompt on every turn. We show that treating decision making within reasonable bounds as an optimization problem, solving it once, and reusing the solved decisions can often make an agent faster, cheaper and more reliable. Our approach, which we call Discretize, Then Decide, starts from data such as the workflow's own logs or, when none exists, runs of the LLM agent itself. It reads each conversation into discrete states and estimates the probability of each outcome and the cost of each move, until no new states appear and the probabilities stop changing. It then solves the resulting Markov decision process. The solution runs as a controller around the model, sending moves whose content is fixed in the state, such as a tool call or a templated reply, and any state it hasn't seen is sent back to the LLM. We call an LLM run this way a Bellman language model (BLM), after Richard Bellman's equation for the best move in each state. On $τ^2$-bench telecom, the controller with no model solves 79% of tasks. As a BLM, Qwen3.8-27B, an open model, goes from 29% to 96% with 93% fewer model calls. For Claude Opus 5.5, which solves 96% of tasks on its own, running it as a BLM cuts model calls and cost per task by about 98% and lets it solve 2 more tasks. On InventoryBench, the solved policy with no model beats every published method. Where the hard part is writing content rather than choosing moves, such as resolving SymPy issues, few decisions can be solved in advance, and a BLM helps little.

title: HSPR: Recovering Software-Agent Benchmark Scores via Hierarchical Posterior Inference
abstract: Evaluating software agents on a full benchmark is expensive. A small task subset can preserve agent rankings while yielding inaccurate scores. Historical responses provide useful structure, but tasks with identical source responses can have different outcomes for a new target agent. We introduce Hierarchical Score Posterior Recovery (HSPR), which combines source-fitted response factors with uncertain group success rates. Observed target outcomes update the posteriors over the target latent state and group rates; posterior-guided acquisition selects subsequent tasks. Its score-based criterion equals the expected one-step reduction in full-score posterior variance. Observed successes and posterior-predictive counts for unqueried tasks yield a full-score posterior. The final estimate uses its median with source-selected calibration. At a 10% task budget on four task banks from the SWE-bench family, HSPR achieves the lowest mean absolute error (MAE) on three banks and the lowest maximum absolute error (MaxErr) on all four among the methods compared. Removing group uncertainty or replacing adaptive queries increases macro MAE in the respective controls. Macro MAE decreases across 5-20% budgets.
