title: Recurrent Temporal Restricted Boltzmann Machines as Unsupervised Encoders for Biomechanical Movement Sequences
abstract: Biomechanical movement recordings are continuous, high-dimensional time series, and analyzing them without manually labeling them requires representations that capture how movements evolve over time. Most unsupervised representation-learning pipelines, however, treat each observation frame independently and discard this temporal structure, while energy-based models that could capture it have not extensively been adapted to biomechanical signals. So, this paper implements the Recurrent Temporal Restricted Boltzmann Machine (RTRBM), a recurrent energy-based model, into an unsupervised encoder that maps windows of movement data to fixed-length embeddings, and tests what its recurrent structure contributes. We adapt the model to continuous-valued signals, stack it into a deep architecture, and integrate it into the SIT-FUSE segmentation pipeline. We evaluate the embeddings on simulated musculoskeletal reaching and on two real gait datasets, using clustering, reconstruction, and walking-speed classification of unseen subjects, and compare them against non-recurrent and non-probabilistic baselines, including a control that removes the recurrent connection. Clustering the embeddings recovers movement structure tied to progress toward the target without any labels, which also transfers to unseen episodes. On gait data, the embeddings outperform PCA and autoencoder baselines under a nonlinear probe. However, removing the recurrent connection does not yield a measurable loss on the reaching task, and simple per-channel summary statistics classify walking speed at least as well as the embeddings. The model is therefore a working, verified encoder for SIT-FUSE, while the evidence for a benefit of recurrence is mixed, and the learned embeddings did not outperform simple summary statistics on gait.

title: NerAxom-MGF: Leveraging Multi-Granularity Fusion for Assamese Named Entity Recognition
abstract: We introduce MGF-NER, a multi-granularity fusion architecture that integrates character-level, subword-level, and entity-span-level representations for the same task using NerAxom dataset. NerAxom comprises 102,857 tokens across 4,178 sentences annotated under the BIO scheme with seven entity categories: Person, Location, Organization, Date, Number, Occupation, and Work-of-Art. MGF-NER combines a Character-level Convolutional Neural Network that captures morpheme-level cues attenuated by subword fragmentation, a pre-trained MuRIL transformer for cross-lingually pretrained contextual semantics, an Entity Span Attention module for multi-word boundary detection, and a Conditional Random Field decoder that enforces valid BIO transitions. Under a seeded five-run evaluation protocol on the NerAxom test set, MGF-NER achieves a mean micro-averaged F1 of 85.45 ± 0.46, outperforming the strongest single-encoder baseline MuRIL (83.88±0.79) by 1.57 F1 points; the improvement is statistically significant under a paired sentence-level Wilcoxon signed-rank test (p = 0.005). We benchmark MGF-NER against nine baselines spanning traditional feature-based sequence labelling (CRF), a recurrent baseline (BiLSTM-CRF), language-agnostic multilingual transformers (mBERT, XLM-RoBERTa base and large, DistilBERT-multi), a script-similar Bangla-specialised transformer (Bangla-BERT), and Indic-specialised transformers (IndicBERTv2). Single-component and compound-component ablations, together with per-category ablation, decompose the gain across the four architectural components, and error analysis characterises the residual error profile.

title: Compose the Horizon: Parameter-Shared Blockwise Forecasting under a Sequential-Compute Trade-off
abstract: Most long-horizon forecasters emit the complete future in one pass. We ask whether a compact operator can instead be reused to emit contiguous future blocks, trading stored parameters for sequential computation. Recursive Functional Decomposition (RFD) factorizes the horizon mapping into three parameter-shared block predictions. The blocks occupy disjoint future intervals and are concatenated, not added as trend, seasonal, or residual components, and each emitted block joins the rolling context that conditions the next application. In controlled three-seed experiments, removing forward feedback hurts all four evaluated datasets while stopping gradients through it changes little, so the useful signal is the evolving forecast state itself; reapplying the shared operator helps consistently, but by less than widening it. The model uses 0.08--0.46M parameters, yet its sequential channel-wise execution is slower and more memory-intensive than an iterative baseline at high channel count. In a frozen long-context evaluation against ten strong baseline families, RFD records lower test error in 23 of 24 cells; the comparison is cross-protocol, with RFD using 512/720-step context and the baselines using 96.

title: VN-MSASar: blind human audit, code and results for auditing LLM-labelled evaluation
abstract: This record accompanies the manuscript "Auditing evaluation on benchmarks annotated by large language models: label noise, source enrichment and design-based correction in multilingual sarcasm and aspect sentiment analysis" (Pham, Huynh and Tran), submitted to Expert Systems: The Journal of Knowledge Engineering. VN-MSASar is a four-language (Vietnamese, English, Chinese, Japanese) benchmark of hotel and restaurant reviews labelled for aspect, sentiment level (-3 to +3) and sarcasm with LLM assistance. This version adds the material needed to check how far scores computed against those machine labels change when the labels are replaced by human judgement. The package contains:- the benchmark splits (8,227 aspect-sentence pairs in the test set);- a blind human audit of 1,500 test pairs, stratified by the machine labels and by data source, with sampling weights and the returned files of four independent annotators;- stored per-example predictions of every evaluated model (fine-tuned encoders and prompted LLMs, with prompts and raw outputs), so no model endpoint has to be called again;- the analysis code that produces every table and figure, including the prediction-powered (PPI) and Horvitz-Thompson estimators, the Shapley decomposition of the enriched versus natural precision gap, and all simulations;- the outputs of every analysis and simulation, with a key_results folder that maps each file to a table or figure of the manuscript. Start with README.md and key_results/README.md. The whole analysis can be rerun with one script (code/analysis/chay_tat_ca_ES.sh) in Python 3.10 with pinned package versions. Review texts were written by users of the source platforms; the authors do not grant redistribution rights over these texts.

VN-MSASar is a four-language (Vietnamese, English, Chinese, Japanese) benchmark of hotel and restaurant reviews labelled for aspect, sentiment level (-3 to +3) and sarcasm with LLM assistance. This version adds the material needed to check how far scores computed against those machine labels change when the labels are replaced by human judgement. The package contains:- the benchmark splits (8,227 aspect-sentence pairs in the test set);- a blind human audit of 1,500 test pairs, stratified by the machine labels and by data source, with sampling weights and the returned files of four independent annotators;- stored per-example predictions of every evaluated model (fine-tuned encoders and prompted LLMs, with prompts and raw outputs), so no model endpoint has to be called again;- the analysis code that produces every table and figure, including the prediction-powered (PPI) and Horvitz-Thompson estimators, the Shapley decomposition of the enriched versus natural precision gap, and all simulations;- the outputs of every analysis and simulation, with a key_results folder that maps each file to a table or figure of the manuscript. Start with README.md and key_results/README.md. The whole analysis can be rerun with one script (code/analysis/chay_tat_ca_ES.sh) in Python 3.10 with pinned package versions. Review texts were written by users of the source platforms; the authors do not grant redistribution rights over these texts.

title: The Self-and-World Model: A General Computational Framework for Adaptive Coordination Between Internal Computation and World-State Modeling
abstract: Computational systems must often coordinate the processing of internal information with the representation of external conditions. A system may perform inference, generate candidate solutions, evaluate alternatives, and select actions while maintaining an internal model of the environment in which those actions will be executed. Although internal computation and world modeling are closely related, they can be designed and evaluated as separate processes. This separation raises a fundamental computational question: how should a system determine whether to devote its resources to improving its internal computation, refining its representation of the world, acquiring additional information, or acting on its current knowledge? This paper proposes the Self-and-World Model (SWM), a general computational framework for adaptively coordinating internal computation with world-state modeling. SWM represents the internal computational state of a system and its world model as distinct but interacting components. Its central principle is that the allocation of internal computation should depend on the adequacy of the current world model, while world-model maintenance should depend on the expected contribution of improved environmental knowledge to subsequent decisions. The framework formalizes internal computational state, world-state representation, uncertainty, prediction error, model updating, action-conditioned prediction, computational cost, and feedback-driven adaptation. It introduces a coupled decision formulation for selecting between internal processing, world-model maintenance, information acquisition, and external action. A reference architecture, a proposed adaptive algorithm, conditional theoretical propositions, complexity considerations, research hypotheses, and a cross-domain evaluation program are presented. SWM is intended as an organizational abstraction for computational systems that must coordinate their internal processing with representations of external conditions. Potential application areas include autonomous agents, robotics, planning, adaptive control, scientific computing, and model-based artificial intelligence. Its proposed contribution is a unified formulation of the relationship between internal computation and world-state modeling. The framework is conceptual and requires systematic comparison with existing research on world models, metareasoning, model-based planning, adaptive computation, and information acquisition to establish its distinctiveness and practical value.

title: The 1CPLT Project: Scaling Up Choreographic Programming
abstract: Abstract Implementing distributed systems is hard. Choreographic programming (CP) is a method that aims to make it easier. The unique selling proposition of the method is that choreographic programs are free of communication deadlocks by construction. However, most existing languages and tools of CP are not scalable: they cannot real(istical)ly be used to implement real(istic) distributed systems, which can be parametric in the number of processes, as well as in the network among them. This paper presents an overview of the 1CPLT project. The long-term vision of the project is to develop the first language and tooling of scalable CP (integrated in VS Code via an LSP server), while continuing to deliver on CP’s original promise: communication deadlock freedom by construction. Previously introduced as a prototype with limited applicability, this paper presents several new features of 1CPLT that bring the vision one step closer. As evidence, this paper presents an implementation of a parametric election algorithm using 1CPLT that could not be implemented using CP before.

title: Teaching Code Agents to Ask Without Leaking Private Code
abstract: Local coding agents can extend their reach by consulting a stronger cloud model. Such consultations, however, often expose the repository's private identifiers, file paths, and source code. Host-side masking hides recognized identifiers but leaves the surrounding code and the agent's phrasing unchanged, while training for less disclosure risks suppressing consultation or producing questions too vague to answer. We propose utility-verified abstraction (UVA), which teaches the agent to describe private entities by their role and type while retaining the technical details an expert needs. From solved repair trajectories, we rewrite each question into this form and keep the rewrite only if it discloses fewer private entities and the repair, replayed from the same execution state with the repair trajectories. Across two benchmarks, the trained agent consults more often than before training. On repository-level issue repair, it solves 37.6% of issues, against 25.3% for the same model working alone, a gain from the training as a whole rather than from consultation alone. Its questions disclose 3.7-fold fewer private entities and 1.4-fold less verbatim code than the untrained agent's questions to the same expert.

title: The Mutual-and-Mutual-and-World Model: A General Computational Framework for Adaptive Coordination Between Interactive Mechanisms and World-State Modeling
abstract: Computational systems increasingly rely on multiple interaction mechanisms and internal representations of the environments in which they operate. Interaction mechanisms enable components to exchange information, aggregate evidence, negotiate constraints, evaluate candidate solutions, and coordinate collective decisions. World models, in contrast, represent aspects of an environment and support the prediction of its possible states, transitions, and consequences under alternative actions. Although both capabilities have been investigated extensively, their coordination creates an additional computational problem: how should a system adaptively organize its interaction mechanisms in relation to its current world model, and how should the outcomes of those interactions influence the subsequent construction, evaluation, and revision of that model? This paper proposes the Mutual-and-Mutual-and-World Model (MMWM), a general computational framework for adaptive coordination between multiple mutual interaction mechanisms and world-state modeling. MMWM extends the interaction-level perspective of the Mutual-and-Mutual Model by explicitly introducing a world-modeling component that represents environmental states, predicts state transitions, estimates uncertainty, and evaluates possible outcomes. The framework treats interaction organization and world-state modeling as coupled but distinguishable computational processes. Interaction mechanisms can provide complementary observations, competing hypotheses, corrections, and verification evidence for world-model construction. Conversely, the world model can guide mechanism selection by estimating environmental uncertainty, predicted consequences, information needs, and the expected value of alternative interaction procedures. The framework is formalized through a world-state representation, an interaction-mechanism space, a mechanism compatibility model, a world-model update operator, a joint adaptive selection policy, and a feedback-driven coordination process. It distinguishes interaction-mechanism selection, mechanism composition, world-model updating, world-model-guided interaction, and joint reconfiguration as separate computational decisions. A reference algorithm and conditional theoretical propositions are presented to clarify the framework's assumptions and potential properties. An experimental program is proposed to evaluate MMWM against fixed interaction mechanisms, fixed world models, independently adaptive interaction and modeling systems, and existing world-model-based planning or coordination methods. MMWM is intended as a general organizational abstraction for investigating how computational systems can coordinate interaction-level adaptation with environment-level representation and prediction. Its practical value, theoretical distinctiveness, and generality require formal analysis, comparison with existing approaches, and reproducible empirical validation.

title: Quantum Teleportation Advances: Energy Transfer via Superconducting Hardware Over 1,400 km — E8 Intelligence Research
abstract: FINDING: Quantum teleportation transfers state (information) not matter; recent experiments extend this to energy teleportation on superconducting hardware over 1,400 km (satellite) and 3-qubit teleportation. | MATH: Core protocol: Bell-state measurement + classical communication (2 bits) + unitary rotation. State transfer fidelity F = |⟨ψ_in|ψ_out⟩|², with F→1 for ideal. Energy teleportation: Hamiltonian H = Σᵢ ωᵢ σᵢᶻ + g Σᵢⱼ σᵢˣσⱼˣ; teleported energy ΔE = ⟨ψ|H_B|ψ⟩ − ⟨0|H_B|0⟩, requires negative conditional energy (entanglement). No mass/energy transport — only correlation. | CONNECTION: No direct ratio (0.382, 0.618, 0.786, 1.618) appears in the cited results. However, the mathematical structure relies on SU(2) symmetry (spin-½), Bell basis (maximally entangled states — 4 orthogonal states in 2⊗2 Hilbert space), and Clifford group operations — all crystallographic in nature (octahedral/tetrahedral symmetry of the Bell basis under local unitary group). title: Pair-Aware Optimization: Coordinating Exploration and Refinement for Jailbreaking LLM Agents
abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) agents are vulnerable to adversarial inputs that induce attacker-specified malicious behaviors, commonly referred to as jailbreaking. Existing optimization-based jailbreak attacks primarily employ first-order (FO) methods that leverage gradient information or zeroth-order (ZO) methods that rely on function-value feedback. However, their complementarity and optimization ordering remain underexplored. We systematically investigate four strategies: pure ZO, pure FO, ZO->FO, and FO->ZO, and develop a ZO-FO framework that explores adversarial prefixes through ZO optimization and refines their corresponding suffixes through FO optimization. To coordinate the two processes, we introduce Pair-aware optimization, which retains multiple prefix candidates, conditionally refines their suffixes and selects among the resulting prefix-suffix pairs. We further investigate agent jailbreaking from a more general stochastic-generation perspective, where the same adversarial input can induce diverse reasoning trajectories and actions that a single greedy output cannot capture. Accordingly, we adopt consistent stochastic decoding during both optimization and evaluation. Experiments across malicious-instruction and malicious-environment benchmarks demonstrate that hybrid optimization improves attack effectiveness over single-optimizer methods, while optimization order substantially influences performance.

title: The Explainability Gap in Enterprise AI
abstract: This conceptual chapter examines how multi-agent enterprise AI can preserve explanations usable in managerial decisions. It draws on technical studies of pipeline failures and traceability, management research on trust and accountability, and selected public vendor documentation. The chapter proposes that loosely coupled handoffs may lose decision-relevant context and justification when systems do not preserve them. The reviewed studies do not establish that managerial explanatory fidelity inevitably declines as agents are added. Instrumented benchmark pipelines can attribute errors using ground truth, but that capability is distinct from providing a justification managers can evaluate in settings with uncertain outcomes or disputed criteria. Illustrative applications in human resources, financial risk and operational planning inform a three-stage diagnostic framework covering input framing, intermediate reasoning and final synthesis. The chapter distinguishes operational traces from faithful explanations, reviews bounded vendor claims, and proposes governance practices for evidence preservation, human intervention and evaluation. Its contribution is a research and management framework, rather than a validated measure of explanatory fidelity or an empirical comparison of enterprise products.

title: Multilingual Language Processing Using Paninian Grammar: Challenges and Future Directions
abstract: The rapid growth of multilingual digital communication has created an urgent need for efficient Natural Language Processing (NLP) systems capable of handling diverse linguistic structures. While modern NLP approaches are increasingly dominated by data-driven and deep learning techniques, linguistic frameworks continue to play a significant role in enhancing language understanding. Among such frameworks, Paninian Grammar, developed by the ancient Indian grammarian Panini, has emerged as a valuable theoretical foundation for multilingual language processing, particularly in morphologically rich and free word-order languages. Paninian Grammar offers a rule-based, dependency-oriented model that focuses on semantic and syntactic relationships among linguistic elements. Its concepts such as Karaka relations, dependency structures, and grammatical transformations provide an effective mechanism for computational analysis of Indian languages and other morphologically complex languages. Over the past few decades, researchers have utilized Paninian principles in machine translation, parsing, information extraction, and multilingual language technologies. Despite its strengths, the application of Paninian Grammar in multilingual language processing faces several challenges, including linguistic diversity, ambiguity resolution, scalability issues, integration with modern neural architectures, and the scarcity of annotated corpora. This paper examines the role of Paninian Grammar in multilingual language processing, discusses its computational significance, analyzes major challenges, and explores future research directions aimed at integrating traditional linguistic knowledge with contemporary artificial intelligence technologies.

title: Efficiency Measured in English: Tokeniser Coverage Bounds Small Language Models on Indic Scripts
abstract: Small Language Models with quantisation and parameter-efficient adaptation are widely offered as the route to multilingual AI under compute constraints, and their efficiency is almost always reported as a single memory figure. We show that this figure is measured in English and does not transfer. Across a 131k-sentence corpus spanning eleven Indic scripts, TinyLlama-1.1B's tokeniser emits 1.34 subword tokens per Latin-script word and 22.60 per Kannada word. This is not inefficiency; it is absence. Its vocabulary contains 0% of Odia's codepoints, 1% of Telugu's and 2% of Kannada's, and for five of eleven scripts the measured fertility sits at the UTF-8 byte-fallback ceiling, on Odia at 99.6% of it, with 93.6% of emitted tokens being raw bytes. Because SentencePiece byte fallback never raises an unknown-token marker, this failure is entirely silent: TinyLlama's UNK rate is 0.0% on every script, including the one it reads as bytes. We further show that low fertility can indicate the opposite of efficiency: mBERT posts its best score anywhere (1.10 tokens/word, on Odia) while discarding 87.9% of the text as UNK. MuRIL, an Indic-vocabulary encoder with a fifth of TinyLlama's parameters, reads every script at 1.23-2.26 tokens/word with zero UNK and zero byte fallback. The binding constraint is the vocabulary, not the parameter count. The consequence is concrete: on a 2048-token context window, the same model gives an English user 1,528 words of usable context and a Kannada user 91.

title: "Readout-Aware Query Accounting for Forward-Only Training of Photonic Meshes: Simulation Data and Code"
abstract: "This dataset provides the numerical evidence and reproducible analysis resources supporting \"Readout-Aware Query Accounting for Forward-Only Training of Photonic Meshes.\" It connects probe-allocation decisions to detector occupancy, capture scheduling, phase writes, settling, input loading, and readout switching, enabling training strategies to be compared using a common physical cost model.The package contains per-seed simulation results, saved mesh states, allocation and timing records, teacher-feature and target caches, frozen study protocols, and computational code. Experiments cover local optical distillation on features derived from MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, and CIFAR-10, with comparisons across readout capacities, allocation strategies, target families, and paired random seeds. The final figures and numerical tables are supplied as references, accompanied by the data-source records used to produce the added main-text figures.A single reproduction entry point rebuilds the reported analyses from archived results and checks them against unchanged reference-output hashes. It also regenerates the final main-text figures and verifies their rendered agreement with the submitted assets. File manifests, a source map, dependency versions, and source-dataset notices support verification and reuse."

title: First-Order LoRA Training with Phone NPUs
abstract: On-device fine-tuning lets a large language model (LLM) learn from its user's private data without uploading it. Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) reduces the trainable parameters, but each first-order training step still multiplies by the frozen base-model weights during the forward pass, activation recomputation, and input-gradient computation. A phone's neural processing unit (NPU) already holds these weights for inference; using it for training also requires computing input gradients, which its inference interface does not support. We present a system that runs all three frozen-weight products on the NPU while keeping the training graph, adapters, and optimizer on the CPU. Its input-gradient kernels reuse the resident weight tiles and the forward dequantizer, avoiding a transposed weight copy and ensuring forward and backward use the same effective weights. To preserve usable gradients, the system selects precision by gradient sensitivity and applies a per-row range guard for half-precision (FP16) outputs. Its runtime fuses the remaining CPU operators and overlaps NPU execution with adapter computation, while resumable execution and thermal pacing let training proceed as a background job. We evaluate it on two Qualcomm Snapdragon platforms using four LLMs from the Qwen and Llama families. Our workloads cover nightly personalization with labels supplied on the phone and the public LaMP-2 benchmark; comparisons include an optimized CPU trainer, a phone-GPU trainer, forward-only training, and GPU-trained references.

title: The hive mind is a single reinforcement learning agent
abstract: Abstract Decision-making is an essential attribute of any intelligent agent or group. Natural systems are known to converge to effective strategies through at least two distinct mechanisms: collective decision-making via imitation of others, and trial-and-error by a single agent. This paper establishes an equivalence between these two paradigms. We show that the emergent distributed cognition (sometimes referred to as the hive mind ) arising from individuals following simple, local imitation-based rules is that of a single online reinforcement learning (RL) agent aggregating action-value samples from many parallel instances of a multi-armed bandit. More specifically, we show that, in the blindly imitative weighted voter model of honey bees’ waggle dance, the update rule through which this macro-agent learns is an RL algorithm that we coin Maynard-Cross Learning . Our analysis implies that a group of individuals following simple imitative strategies can be equivalent to a more complex learning entity, substantiating the idea that group-level intelligence may explain how seemingly irrational individual behaviors are selected in nature. Beyond biology, the framework offers new tools for analyzing economic and social systems where individuals imitate successful strategies, effectively participating in a collective learning process. Our findings may further inform the design of scalable RL-inspired collective systems in artificial domains.

title: The Self-and-Mutual Structure Model: A General Computational Framework for Adaptive Structural Organization and Reorganization in Multiple Large Language Models
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) and other computational systems depend not only on the quality of their individual processing mechanisms but also on the structures through which computational operations, information, tasks, and decision-making responsibilities are organized. Within a single model or computational agent, internal task decomposition, processing stages, dependency relationships, and module arrangements determine how individual operations are coordinated. Across multiple models or agents, centralized, decentralized, hierarchical, and parallel structures determine how information is exchanged, responsibilities are distributed, and intermediate results are integrated. However, a fixed structure may be inefficient when task requirements change, while frequent structural reorganization may introduce additional computation, communication overhead, coordination instability, and unnecessary complexity. This paper proposes the Self-and-Mutual Structure Model (SMSM), a conceptual computational framework for adaptively organizing and reorganizing internal computational structures and inter-agent coordination structures. The framework distinguishes self-structural mechanisms, which organize operations within an individual computational entity, from mutual-structural mechanisms, which organize relationships among multiple entities. A structure-aware controller evaluates task requirements, dependency patterns, uncertainty, structural bottlenecks, communication costs, resource constraints, and historical structural performance to select, retain, modify, or replace an appropriate organization. The framework supports transitions among alternative internal structures, communication topologies, task-allocation patterns, and hybrid configurations. It formulates structural adaptation as a constrained sequential decision problem and introduces a cost-sensitive objective balancing task quality, reliability, computational expenditure, latency, and structural reorganization costs. A reference architecture, formal problem definition, adaptive algorithm, research hypotheses, and experimental protocol are presented. The framework is a research proposal rather than an empirically validated system. Because adaptive multi-agent communication topology and structural reorganization have already been investigated in prior work, the principal research question is whether a unified controller that explicitly connects individual computational organization with inter-agent organization can provide measurable advantages over existing structural adaptation methods.

title: SL-Ground: Sentence-Level Grounding for Fine-Grained Open-Vocabulary Object Detection
abstract: Grounding-based open-vocabulary detectors provide a widely used framework for text-conditioned localization, with a phrase-grounding formulation that aligns object queries to individual text tokens and recovers class scores through token-to-class aggregation. We observe that this token-level scoring design becomes a bottleneck for fine-grained open-vocabulary object detection, where the target category is defined by a complete compositional description rather than by isolated tokens. Based on this observation, we propose SL-Ground, a sentence-level grounding reformulation for grounding-based open-vocabulary detection. Instead of scoring queries against fragmented token evidence, SL-Ground encodes each category description as a complete sentence-level representation and directly scores object queries against these representations. To evaluate fine-grained recognition across label granularity, we construct a multi-granularity Stanford Cars benchmark spanning vehicle type, brand, and car model. At the finest car-model granularity, SL-Ground raises AP over the token-level variant from 14.5 to 70.6 under matched training candidate sampling and to 86.0 with full-vocabulary training, while better preserving open-vocabulary capability and avoiding repeated prompt chunking. Beyond Stanford Cars, SL-Ground also improves FG-OVD performance, achieving the best average AP among compared methods. These results show that sentence-level grounding provides a more suitable scoring unit for fine-grained OVOD and offers a practical path toward fine-grained grounding-based open-vocabulary detectors.

title: RegCL: Compact Continual SAM Adaptation for Visual Grounding in Multi-Sensorial Media
abstract: Multi-sensorial media systems, including AR/VR, remote operation, and embodied AI, require visual grounding modules that remain reliable as sensing environments and application domains evolve. The Segment Anything Model (SAM) provides a strong foundation for dense visual segmentation, but its performance degrades on specialized and dynamically arriving domains such as medical imagery, camouflaged scenes, and shadow-dominant environments. Existing continual learning methods often rely on replay data or growing domain-specific modules, limiting compact deployment in evolving media pipelines. To address this issue, we propose RegCL, a non-replay continual adaptation framework that consolidates multi-domain segmentation knowledge into a single SAM adapter through incremental model merging. RegCL merges lightweight adaptation modules, e.g., LoRA-style AugModules, by optimizing prediction consistency between the merged model and domain-specific adapters while carrying forward compact historical feature statistics. Experiments across five heterogeneous segmentation datasets show that RegCL achieves strong retention and adaptation under domain-incremental learning, outperforming competitive non-replay continual learning and merging baselines. These results suggest that RegCL can serve as a compact visual adaptation component for evolving multi-sensorial media pipelines. The code is available at https://github.com/Anderw-S/RegCL

title: EarthScienceKit: inspectable Earth-system computations
abstract: First release on PyPI, with the git history on GitHub, CI, tag-driven releases (release.yml), docs hosted on GitHub Pages (docs.yml), a mypy step in CI, JupyterLite buttons on the gallery and a Colab quickstart notebook (ROADMAP item 1). New geophysics domain (ROADMAP item 6): gravity anomalies and reductions, normal gravity, Clairaut's theorem and the flattening, satellite J2, Stokes's geoid kernel, the axial dipole and zonal Gauss coefficients, field elements, virtual geomagnetic poles, magnetic anomalies of reversed blocks, the dynamo scales, Love numbers and GRACE equivalent water: 30 algebraic models and the dynamic simulate_rikitake_dynamo. Its history is a dated chronology of 16 breakthroughs, from Gilbert's magnetic Earth (1600) to GRACE (2002), each with its own executed example. New units m/s^2, mGal, T and nT. New volcanology domain (ROADMAP item 7): radioactive decay and the age equation, radiocarbon, Pb-Pb ages, the U-Pb concordia and the isochron, Rayleigh fractionation and delta values, fractional and equilibrium crystallization, lattice-strain partitioning, the oxygen-isotope thermometer, Arrhenius and Shaw viscosity, water solubility, dike ascent, the Mogi source, plume and eruption-column heights and the VEI: 23 algebraic models and the dynamic simulate_eruption_column. Its history is a dated chronology of 17 breakthroughs, from Rayleigh's fractional distillation (1896) to the Volcanic Explosivity Index (1982), each with its own executed example. New units kyr, Ma, Ga and GPa; new constants AVOGADRO, LAMBDA_U238, LAMBDA_U235, U238_U235 and LIBBY_MEAN_LIFE. Family layout: each domain is a package of systems/ .py modules with core/, visualizers/ and tests/; constants and units are packages and the cross-cutting tests moved from tests/ to earthsciencekit/tests/. Every public import path, such as from earthsciencekit.climate import simulate_one_box, is unchanged. plate_tectonics history is a dated chronology of 16 breakthroughs, from Euler's rotation theorem (1776) to NUVEL-1 (1990), each with its own executed example; the three shared plate_tectonics gallery scripts are removed. New plate_tectonics models: mantle_rayleigh_number, flexural_deflection, hotspot_age, ocean_depth and compose_euler_vectors. seismology history is a dated chronology of 16 breakthroughs, from Poisson's two elastic waves (1829) to PREM (1981), each with its own executed example; the three shared seismology gallery scripts are removed. New seismology models: rayleigh_wave_speed, head_wave_travel_time, crossover_distance, love_wave_angular_frequency, ray_parameter, local_magnitude and vertical_travel_time. atmosphere history is a dated chronology of 16 breakthroughs, from Torricelli's barometer (1643) to the ENIAC forecast (1950), each with its own executed example; the three shared atmosphere gallery scripts are removed. New atmosphere models: barometer_column_height, two_layer_temperature, richardson_number, surface_pressure_tendency, rossby_wave_speed and the dynamic simulate_barotropic_vorticity. climate history is a dated chronology of 16 breakthroughs, from Fourier's greenhouse (1824) to the sea-level budget (2005), each with its own executed example; the three shared climate gallery scripts are removed. New climate models: greenhouse_surface_temperature, daily_insolation, radiative_convective_temperature, equilibrium_solar_constant, red_noise_spectrum, methane_forcing, nitrous_oxide_forcing and gregory_regression. oceanography history is a dated chronology of 16 breakthroughs, from Newton's equilibrium tide (1687) to TEOS-10 (2010), each with its own executed example; the three shared oceanography gallery scripts are removed. New oceanography models: gerstner_orbit_radius, ekman_spiral_velocity, sverdrup_transport, stommel_streamfunction, thermohaline_forcing, abyssal_temperature, simplified_seawater_density and the dynamic simulate_thermohaline_boxes.

title: Retrieval-Grounded, Distractor-Robust Quantitative Reasoning with a Local Small Language Model: A System Report for DocSem 2026
abstract: We describe a three-stage pipeline submitted to the DocSem 2026 shared task on document-grounded quantitative reasoning with evidence attribution. Each task instance provides a scanned, image-only PDF containing a self-contained arithmetic word problem embedded among a large number of lexically similar but irrelevant distractor passages, together with a heavily templated, low-information user query. Our system (i) performs OCR-based document parsing with error-tolerant block-identifier recovery, (ii) locates the evidence-bearing block using a small set of deterministic discourse-marker regular expressions rather than dense or semantic retrieval, and (iii) solves the located problem with a local 3B-parameter instruction-tuned language model, comparing free-form chain-of-thought self-consistency against program-aided (code-execution) solving. On a held-out development sample of 40 instances, program-aided solving reached 70% answer accuracy against 47.5% for chain-of-thought self-consistency, while evidence-block retrieval reached 100% across every development sample we evaluated (n > 60). We report several empirical findings of independent interest: (a) conclusions drawn from small evaluation samples (n=15) were reversed by a larger sample (n=40), underscoring the risk of underpowered pipeline comparisons; (b) the held-out test split used a materially different block-identifier format and evidence-marker vocabulary than the training and validation splits, which we interpret as a deliberate probe for retrieval logic that has overfit to surface patterns rather than task semantics; and (c) compute constraints on free consumer hardware limited our final test submission to 125 of 1,730 instances, and, on direct inspection of the submitted file, the resulting 0.00% official test score appears attributable primarily to exact-match evidence scoring failing against OCR-corrupted short alphanumeric identifiers rather than to wholesale pipeline or model failure, since 96% of completed instances received substantive (non-placeholder) answers. We discuss this outcome honestly, including the evidence supporting that diagnosis, and argue that both the operational lesson, inference throughput under a fixed compute budget is as consequential as per-instance accuracy, and the scoring-sensitivity finding, exact-match evidence metrics may be a poor discriminator of system quality when evidence identifiers are OCR-derived, are useful contributions independent of our final rank.

We report several empirical findings of independent interest: (a) conclusions drawn from small evaluation samples (n=15) were reversed by a larger sample (n=40), underscoring the risk of underpowered pipeline comparisons; (b) the held-out test split used a materially different block-identifier format and evidence-marker vocabulary than the training and validation splits, which we interpret as a deliberate probe for retrieval logic that has overfit to surface patterns rather than task semantics; and (c) compute constraints on free consumer hardware limited our final test submission to 125 of 1,730 instances, and, on direct inspection of the submitted file, the resulting 0.00% official test score appears attributable primarily to exact-match evidence scoring failing against OCR-corrupted short alphanumeric identifiers rather than to wholesale pipeline or model failure, since 96% of completed instances received substantive (non-placeholder) answers. We discuss this outcome honestly, including the evidence supporting that diagnosis, and argue that both the operational lesson, inference throughput under a fixed compute budget is as consequential as per-instance accuracy, and the scoring-sensitivity finding, exact-match evidence metrics may be a poor discriminator of system quality when evidence identifiers are OCR-derived, are useful contributions independent of our final rank.

title: paperlab-space: no-code LLM evaluation on spreadsheet data
abstract: paperlab-space is the open-source engine behind PaperLab.space. It evaluates large language models on researchers' own Excel or CSV data and produces paper-ready results: per-row outputs and scores in Excel, a LaTeX comparison table, and a reproducibility config recording model versions, prompts, seeds, metric settings, and a hash of the data. It supports many providers through LiteLLM, rate-limit-aware runs with retries and resume, and metrics that handle non-Latin scripts such as Burmese, Thai, Chinese, and Japanese.

title: Tilted Mondrian: Triage and Mitigation of Fine-grained Disparities in Conformal Prediction
abstract: Fairness in conformal prediction is often pursued through Mondrian calibration, which provides finite-sample coverage guarantees separately across groups. These guarantees, however, are coarse: substantial disparities can remain within finer strata. This coarse-to-fine fairness issue raises two questions: how severe can such disparities be, and how can they be mitigated? Aggregate disparities can depend on how groups are distributed across strata. For severity assessment, we introduce propensity standardization to examine the effect of population composition, and show how group composition can induce disagreement between aggregate and finer-stratum comparisons. For mitigation, we develop Tilted Mondrian to improve fairness compared to group-Mondrian at a finer level without additional model training. Tilted Mondrian retains groupwise coverage guarantees and mitigates coverage and prediction set size disparities within finer strata. Finally, we derive a method-agnostic bound that quantifies how much reduction in finer-stratum coverage disparity can be achieved.

title: Realisation of a protected cat-qutrit manifold via engineered quantum tunnelling
abstract: Engineering quantum tunnelling in phase space has emerged as a viable method for creating a protected logical qubit manifold with biased-noise properties. A promising approach is to combine a Kerr nonlinearity with a multi-photon drive, resulting in a system known as a Kerr parametric oscillator (KPO). In this work, we implement a three-photon KPO and explore its potential as a protected bosonic qutrit. We confirm quantum coherence by demonstrating three-photon Rabi oscillations and performing direct Wigner function measurements that reveal the formation of three-component cat-like states. Crucially, we observe a breathing-like dynamic in phase space, a characteristic feature of driven quantum systems. This dynamic arises from macroscopic temporal interference between the cat-qutrit manifold and the excited states. The frequency of resulting oscillations in the mean photon number provides a direct, time-domain measurement of the energy gap separating the qutrit from the excited states, thereby establishing an experimental hallmark of qutrit manifold protection. Furthermore, we identify a parasitic higher-order pump term as the primary mechanism constraining the mean photon number, highlighting its mitigation as a requisite for maximising protection. Our findings elucidate the basic quantum properties of the three-photon KPO and establish the first step towards its use as an alternative qutrit platform.

title: Raw Qubit-Use Architecture for Superconducting Magic State Cultivation and Grafting: Conjugate Sublattice Allocation, Exact Qubit-Lifetime DAG Scheduling, Subspace-Tagged Qutrit Leakage Clamping, and Elastic Ring-Buffer Tiling
authors: solidSF Research Team: using Jesse v1.2.16
abstract: We present a mathematical and architectural analysis of physical qubit utilization in superconducting magic state cultivation and surface-code grafting on Google Quantum AI's Willow processor (arXiv:2512.13908v1), identifying five hardware-level qubit-use bottlenecks that limit post-selected yield and grafted memory fidelity and proving five architectural resolutions mechanized across 26 theorems in the Lean 4 theorem prover (JesseMath/Physics/WillowQubitCultivationArch.lean, verified by the compile-time metaprogramming linter JesseMath/Linter/AxiomAudit.lean via #assert_zfc_axioms with zero sorry declarations, and zero custom axioms beyond ZFC, paired with 2,280 deterministic assertions in harness/willow_qubit_cultivation_arch_oracle.py). Conjugate Fixed-Role Sublattice Grafting and Weight-6 Gauge Splitting (6 Theorems, 390 Oracle Checks): Initializing the 13-qubit d = 3 color code on the conjugate sublattice of the 54-qubit d = 5 grafted surface code eliminates the mid-circuit data/measure role swap (roleSwap) during the Extend stage, driving swap-induced readout-collision |2⟩ leakage identically to zero (conjugate_graft_zero_role_swaps, conjugate_graft_eliminates_swap_leakage), while splitting the two weight-6 interface plaquettes via one gauge ancilla reduces check weight 6 → 4 (8 → 6 two-qubit gate layers) and restores graphlike syndrome hyperedge degree 3 → 2 (weight6_gauge_split_restores_matchability). Exact Min-Peak Qubit-Lifetime DAG Scheduling and Step-7 Fast Abort Recycling (7 Theorems, 1,653 Oracle Checks): We prove the active-qubit conservation law W(t) + (t − 1) = R(t) (active_qubits_conservation_law), show that measurement-reset reordering reduces active d = 5 surface-code simulation memory from 49 to 26 qubits (saving 23 qubits / 223 statevector factor in surface_code_d5_saves_23_qubits), establish a strict separation on a 5-measurement, 7-reset flagged QEC DAG where kraus-sim's 0-lookahead greedy heuristic requires peak 4 active qubits while the exact amortized-release schedule requires peak 3 qubits (exact_scheduler_strictly_beats_greedy), and prove that aborting rejected ĤL = −1 trajectories at Step 7 compresses mean attempt duration from 6.0 to 4.25 cycles (114.0 → 80.75 qubit-cycles, 1.4118× throughput gain in step7_fast_abort_reduces_qubit_cycles). Full-Codespace Stabilizer Sandwiching and Frame-Balanced Echoes (4 Theorems, 50 Oracle Checks): We resolve the Section IX coherent tomography discrepancy between the rounded printed norm 0.65302 + (−0.7588)2 = 1.00218644 ≈ 1.0022 and the unrounded X-post-selected norm 0.652529142 + (−0.75883684)2 = 1.00162756 ≈ 1.0016 via exact 128-dimensional statevector analysis (mismatched_postselection_exceeds_unit_sphere, section_ix_printed_vs_exact_norm_reconciliation), prove that full-codespace stabilizer sandwiching (ΠC = ΠXΠZ) restores unit norm ||rΠC||22 = 1 (full_codespace_sandwich_restores_physical_norm), and prove that symmetric Pauli-X echoes annihilate static detuning (2.46 × 105× variance suppression in balanced_echo_annihilates_static_detuning). Subspace-Tagged Qutrit CLE Simulation (qevol-leak) and Interleaved DQLR Clamping (5 Theorems, 55 Oracle Checks): Decomposing the n-qutrit state space into ⨁|L|≤ℓmax HL with punctured computational tableau size n − |L| (punctured_tableau_qubit_count) and degraded fault distance d − 2|L| (leaked_qubits_degrade_fault_distance), we prove that unmitigated leakage grows linearly (unmitigated_leakage_grows_linearly) whereas swap-free Data-Qubit Leakage Removal (DQLR) clamps steady-state leakage at L∞ = γleak/ηLRU = 0.235% (dqlr_clamps_steady_state_leakage, swap_free_dqlr_strictly_reduces_graft_error), reducing d = 5 grafted cycle error from 5.30%/cycle to 0.72%/cycle. Two-Tier Complementary Soft-Gap Routing and Elastic Ring-Buffer Tiling (4 Theorems, 132 Oracle Checks): Salvaging moderate-gap shots (6 dB ≤ Δgap < 12 dB) into a Tier-2 single-stage distillation buffer expands usable Willow yield from 8.0% to 14.5% (two_tier_soft_gap_increases_yield), shrinking the parallel 19-qubit micro-cultivator pool from 15 lanes (285 qubits) to 9 lanes (171 qubits, saving 114 transmons in soft_gap_reduces_cultivator_lane_footprint), while a depth-B ring buffer suppresses consumption stall probability exponentially as (1 − ρ)ρB (ring_buffer_exponential_starvation_decay) and single-stage distillation of p3 cultivated inputs achieves ninth-order error scaling 35(C3p3)3 = 35C33p9 = 1.50 × 10−12 with a 4.33× to 12.78× spacetime volume reduction (single_stage_cultivation_beats_two_stage_volume).

title: Is Wireless Security Ready for the AI Era? Evidence from a Curated Corpus of 130 Studies, 2020–2026
abstract: Machine learning (ML) is now central to published radio-link authentication research — and simultaneously the adversary’s standard toolkit. This scoping review classifies 130 curated studies (2020–2026): a 121-study core on ML for wireless-link security or attacks on it (84 defense, 30 threat, 7 dual attack-plus-defense), plus 9 post- quantum-cryptography studies in a separate stratum. Each study is coded on six fields — security function, AI method, track, data source, validation practice, and readiness (R1–R5) — by a single coder and independently validated by a second author. Validation practice splits by kind: 16 of 30 threat studies demonstrate on testbeds or over theair, while simulation-only and standard-split evaluations carry much of the defense mass; closed-loop evaluation appears in 14 of 121 core studies (11.6%). Reproducibility is near- absent (4 verified artifact releases, 3.3%), and standards alignment outside the post-quantum stratum is mention-level only (9.9%). Real-time, update, and multi-agent-trust requirements are essentially unaddressed (1–2 papers each). Because 110 of 130 rows were coded from abstracts by a single coder, cross-group comparisons are indicative rather than measured effects. The paper releases the classified dataset for independent checking, distills six structural research gaps, and closes with a twelve-item reporting checklist (WIRELESS-AI-RC)

title: Directionally Factorized Illumination with Spherical Harmonic Rotation
abstract: Many real-world capture scenarios involve an active light source rigidly attached to the camera: camera flashes for dark-environment imaging, underwater vehicle lights, and endoscopic/laparoscopic medical procedures. As the camera moves, the co-mounted light moves with it, causing the illumination direction at each surface point to change across views. Neural rendering methods (NeRF, Gaussian Splatting) encode this pose-dependent illumination as surface coloration, producing appearance inconsistencies and making it harder to recover the underlying scene. We present \textbf{DaFISH}, which can be plugged into any novel-view synthesis (NVS) pipeline such as NeRF. It factorizes per-point emitted color into surface albedo and a spherical harmonic (SH)-represented illumination factor. During training, the SH illumination is evaluated directly, enabling stable joint optimization of albedo, lighting, and geometry. \textbf{DaFISH} provides analytical generalization of illumination to arbitrary camera poses without retraining. Building on the closed-form SH-to-irradiance conversion, the training pipeline is fully differentiable from SH evaluation through volume rendering. Averaged over the held-out frames of the five scenes, \textbf{DaFISH} attains the best mean PSNR (38.91\,dB), SSIM (0.9613), and LPIPS (0.0582) among all compared methods. It improves over the strongest splatting baseline as well as the closest NeRF-based baseline, while recovering the scene consistently across views compared to prior methods.

title: Lowering the Barrier to International Publishing: AI-Assisted Publication-Readiness Assessment for Central Asian Researchers
abstract: Researchers in Central Asia usually think and write in Uzbek, Russian or Kazakh but must publish in English or in venues with strict formal requirements, and higher-education reform has multiplied the number of manuscripts expected of them. Tools that could help are scarce for Uzbek, and general-purpose language models make confident but wrong corrections. This paper presents Imlox, a publication-readiness report that combines a deterministic Uzbek language core with a large language model (Claude Haiku 4.5) used only as a bounded verifier. All evaluation is synthetic: errors were injected into held-out sentences, and thresholds and test sets were pre-registered and sealed. On the first sealed set (30 September 2026), a naive union of core and model reached a precision of only 0.463 and failed its gate. After the model's role was restricted, a second sealed set of 330 sentences with 221 injected errors gave precision of 0.895 to 0.906 and recall of 0.674 to 0.810; a fourth run's recall fell to 0.624. By 17 October 2026, 476 manuscripts had received readiness reports in shadow mode. A tightly bounded model can raise recall in a low-resource language without sacrificing precision, but recall is not yet stable. The figures are preliminary.

title: Ask, Don't Guess: Targeted Clarification for Speech Recognition Errors
abstract: Speech recognition in real time in far-field conversational settings still incurs significant errors. Identifying potential error spans during streaming ASR permits a recourse mechanism where the speaker can be asked to repeat the affected content under cleaner acoustic conditions. We propose \sysname, a new framework for online error localization, that identifies spans likely to benefit from this intervention. Our supervision uses clean audio to estimate how the recognizer's output might change under improved acoustic conditions. We probabilistically align noisy and clean decodes using a pair-HMM to obtain soft supervision. These soft targets train a counterfactual gain scorer by combining a suite of acoustic and language features to produce token-level scores, that are further grouped into spans for targeted recourse. An LLM uses the ASR transcript of the repetition to revise only the selected span. At a precision of $70\%$, \sysname achieves the highest recall by identifying up to 52\% more erroneous tokens compared to the strongest baseline. Targeted repetition yields relative WER reductions of up to 24\% under a budget that accounts for both interruption frequency and the lengths of re-uttered spans.

At a precision of $70\%$, \sysname achieves the highest recall by identifying up to 52\% more erroneous tokens compared to the strongest baseline. Targeted repetition yields relative WER reductions of up to 24\% under a budget that accounts for both interruption frequency and the lengths of re-uttered spans.

title: Topological Multilingual Parsing in a Single 64-Bit Register: How the 39-Trit Shingari Grimoire and 13-Tooth Chromatic Gear Decompose the 53-Variant Section 1557 Rosetta Corpus
abstract: Contemporary natural language processing architectures rely on probabilistic subword tokenization schemes—such as Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE) and WordPiece—that fragment morphological structure across non-Western and indigenous languages while incurring massive floating-point energy dissipation. In this monograph, we present a deterministic, low-dimensional topological alternative engineered for Dandelion OS (v2.0.0), a real-time PREEMPT_RT Linux fork stabilized by a triadic digital fly-by-wire loop between a Human Operator (-1 Blue / Schwer), an OS Kernel Mediator (0 Green / Treaty Line), and an Embedded Ternary AI Co-Pilot (+1 Red / Shin). Using an empirical 53-variant parallel corpus from a statutory Section 1557 healthcare language assistance notice (Document ID 161730-286-29823114)[cite: 1, 2] spanning 16 writing systems and 13 major linguistic families—including Polysynthetic Iroquoian (Cherokee), Muskogean (Choctaw), Na-Dene (Navajo), Bantu, Kru, Afroasiatic, Austronesian, Austroasiatic, Tai-Kadai, Hmong-Mien, Dravidian, Sino-Tibetan, and Indo-European branches—we demonstrate that every surface realization of the invariant proposition can be parsed and normalized by a 39-trit balanced ternary Grimoire descriptor ($G \in \{-1, 0, +1\}^{13 \times 3}$). Grouped into a 4-5-4 Gaiku modifier cadence and routed through a 13-Tooth Chromatic Language Gear centered on Greek at $(0,0,0)$, the entire 39-trit syntactic-semantic state requires only $39 \log_2(3) \approx 61.8135$ bits, fitting inside a single 64-bit hardware register (uint64_t). Finally, we show how Row 12 of the Shingari header autonomously detects and repairs six real-world typesetting and OCR corruptions in the physical corpus.

title: Medical Fine-Tuning Reshapes, Not Reduces, Patient-Facing AI Risk: A Rubric-Based, LLM-Judge Evaluation Framework
abstract: Patient-facing medical question answering with large language models (LLMs) is moving from research demonstrations to production deployments, yet evaluation remains anchored on factual correctness. Factuality is necessary but not sufficient: a response can be factually grounded and still issue a directive that, if acted on, would harm the patient. We introduce a risk-sensitive evaluation framework that scores responses by the presence and severity of six categories of risk-bearing language (treatment directives, contraindications, dosage expressions, urgency-triage cues, high-alert medication mentions, and overconfident assertions), anchored on published clinical harm taxonomies. Severity is classified by a three-judge LLM ensemble. We apply this framework to six 7-9B instruction-tuned models, three general (Mistral-7B, Phi-3.5-mini, Llama-3.1-8B) and three medically adapted (BioMistral-7B, OpenBioLLM-Llama3-8B, Med42-Llama3-8B), on 200 real patient questions from the K-QA benchmark. Two findings emerge. First, ensemble risk-bearing language is statistically independent of factual hallucination rate (pooled Spearman $ρ= -0.065$, $n = 300$, 95% CI $[-0.18, +0.05]$; distance correlation $= 0.10$, independence test $p = 0.24$). Second, medical fine-tuning does not reduce aggregate risk but reshapes it: continued-pretraining adaptations (BioMistral, OpenBioLLM) consistently suppress high-alert medication mentions while amplifying overconfident assertions, whereas clinical instruction-tuning (Med42) suppresses dosing only, without amplifying overconfidence. Per-category Krippendorff $α$ is fair to good for the four linguistically anchored categories (0.53-0.71) and low for the two clinical-judgment-dependent categories (0.19, 0.31), indicating where automatic safety evaluation is and is not yet reliable. We release the rubric, judge prompts, and evaluation code.

title: Trinary Nine-Dimensional Cognitive Coordinate System: A Locatable and Generalizable Symbolic Cognition Layer
abstract: This paper proposes a cognitive coordinate layer built on a deterministic symbolic system: the Trinary Nine-Dimensional Cognitive Coordinate System. The system uses three yao states—yin (-1), zhong (0, neutral), and yang (+1)—to form nine-dimensional ordered vectors, yielding a state space of 3^9 = 19,683 gua (symbolic states). Four structural operators—inversion, reversal, mutual-kernel projection, and changing-yao—together with equivalence-class rules produce 5,002 independent equivalence groups. Euclidean distance supports natural-language situation to coordinate, then to neighborhood retrieval, enabling both localization and generalization. We construct a semantic bridge that validates the hypothesis that gua with the same index denote the same situation across domains, across five semantic domains—essence-function-change, Luoshu nine-palace, Xiao Liu Ren, healing, and a human gua canon—with a sampled mechanical consistency of 12/12. A 19,683-entry human gua canon provides deep symbolic interpretation, mapping symbolic coordinates back into human language. Finally, we encapsulate the cognition layer as an Agent-callable tool registry and hybridize it with a large language model, realizing an intelligent-agent cognitive aid that can both locate and generalize. Keywords: trinary nine-dimensional; symbolic system; cognitive coordinate; semantic bridge; neighborhood generalization; Agent cognition layer.

title: Is User Calibration Still Necessary for Continuous Myoelectric Control? A Closed-Loop Comparison of Calibration-Free Controllers
abstract: The need for user-specific calibration remains an often-cited barrier to widespread adoption of myoelectric control. Cross-user models trained on large multi-user datasets can now recognize gestures from unseen users without calibration, but they have been evaluated almost exclusively offline, leaving open whether calibration is still needed in closed-loop control. This study compared six calibration-free controllers, trained on 306 users of the EMG-EPN-612 dataset and used without any calibration data from the test participant, against three calibrated controllers in a closed-loop Fitts' law target-acquisition task with sixteen participants. The calibrated controllers achieved higher offline balanced accuracy (90.6% against 73.1% for the best controller of each paradigm), but completion rates did not differ significantly between paradigms, and the highest completion rate was achieved by a calibration-free controller. Calibrated controllers moved faster on successful acquisitions, partly because of their individually fitted speed mappings, though not significantly after correction for multiple comparisons. However, every calibration-free controller produced more direct and stable trajectories than every calibrated controller, even after adjusting for cursor speed. Offline accuracy did not predict completion rate across controllers or within participants, and across paradigms higher offline accuracy was associated with poorer trajectory quality in 15 of 16 participants. Without any calibration data from the end user, a model trained across a large population matched calibrated control in completion rate and exceeded it in trajectory quality. The offline accuracy gained through calibration should therefore not be taken as evidence of a closed-loop benefit.

title: Supplementary Material S1 and Supplementary Data S2 for "Goal-Relative Evidence Recovery for Trajectory Anomaly Detection"
abstract: This record contains the supplementary materials for the manuscript "Goal-Relative Evidence Recovery for Trajectory Anomaly Detection". Supplementary Material S1 provides expanded evaluation protocols, complete quality results, runtime and resource accounting, development and model-selection details, component diagnostics, paired uncertainty analyses, and reproducibility and archive provenance. Supplementary Data S2 provides the full-precision companion tables, the complete 98-endpoint development record, current component tables, frozen aggregate summaries, and a data dictionary. The associated implementation, pretrained model states, and TEST input reconstruction instructions are available in the GERTAD repository. The original GeoLife 1.3 archive and reconstructed trajectory coordinate arrays are not redistributed; GeoLife and provider-derived map materials remain subject to their respective source terms.

title: Table Serialization Determines Which Relations Language Models Preserve
abstract: We study how text serialization affects table lookup in instruction-tuned language models. Our diagnostic asks the model to find the row containing a specified value under one named column, then return the value under another named column in that same row. We render the same synthetic 256-cell tables in row-major form and in column-major form with each header placed beside its values, while varying the table aspect ratio across five shapes. Across three models, the better format changes with table shape: row-major performs better on tall tables, whereas column-major performs better on wide tables. At 64 x 4, row-major leads by 42.3-54.0 percentage points; at 4 x 64, column-major leads by 35.0-59.0 points. Mapping wrong answers back to their source cells reveals a complementary error pattern: row-major tends to preserve the correct row but lose the target column, while column-major tends to preserve the correct column but lose the row. We use the term relational locality to describe this pattern: serialization keeps one relation locally available while making the other depend on positional alignment. A separate non-tabular ordering experiment supports this interpretation. Thus, apparent width-related failures in text-serialized tables depend on linearization, not table shape alone.

title: The Mutual-and-World Model: A General Computational Framework for Adaptive Coordination Between Mutual Interaction and World-State Modeling
abstract: Computational systems increasingly depend on both interactions among multiple computational components and internal representations of the environments in which they operate. Mutual interaction enables components to exchange information, combine observations, compare hypotheses, resolve disagreements, and coordinate decisions. World models represent environmental states and dynamics, allowing systems to estimate current conditions, predict future states, and evaluate the consequences of alternative actions. Although these capabilities serve different functions, their effectiveness may depend on how they are coordinated. A world model can identify uncertainties that require additional interaction, while interaction-generated evidence can support the evaluation and revision of that model. This paper proposes the Mutual-and-World Model (MWM), a general computational framework for adaptive coordination between mutual interaction and world-state modeling. The framework treats mutual interaction and world modeling as distinct but interdependent computational processes. It formalizes how a system can use world-state estimates, predictive uncertainty, and anticipated environmental consequences to determine whether interaction is necessary, which interaction procedure should be activated, and how much interaction is justified. It also formalizes how information generated through interaction can be evaluated and incorporated into a world model without assuming that agreement among components necessarily establishes environmental truth. MWM is specified through a computational component representation, an interaction operator, a world-state model, an interaction activation policy, a world-model update operator, and a joint decision objective. A reference algorithm describes the coordination process, while conditional propositions identify circumstances under which adaptive coordination may improve expected utility, preserve evidence validity, and reduce unnecessary interaction. evidence.title: The Mutual-and-World Model: A General Computational Framework for Adaptive Coordination Between Mutual Interaction and World-State Modeling
evidence.abstract: Computational systems increasingly depend on both interactions among multiple computational components and internal representations of the environments in which they operate. Mutual interaction enables components to exchange information, combine observations, compare hypotheses, resolve disagreements, and coordinate decisions. World models represent environmental states and dynamics, allowing systems to estimate current conditions, predict future states, and evaluate the consequences of alternative actions. Although these capabilities serve different functions, their effectiveness may depend on how they are coordinated. A world model can identify uncertainties that require additional interaction, while interaction-generated evidence can support the evaluation and revision of that model. The framework treats mutual interaction and world modeling as distinct but interdependent computational processes. It formalizes how a system can use world-state estimates, predictive uncertainty, and anticipated environmental consequences to determine whether interaction is necessary, which interaction procedure should be activated, and how much interaction is justified. It also formalizes how information generated through interaction can be evaluated and incorporated into a world model without assuming that agreement among components necessarily establishes environmental truth. title: Who Gets Unmasked? Sampler-Induced Bias in Diffusion Language Models
abstract: Diffusion language models (dLLMs) generate by gradually unmasking a canvas, so their samplers decide not only which token to write but also when to commit it. We show that this second decision changes who appears in generated text, a sampler-induced bias on top of the model's own. Common commit rules, including LLaDA's default, commit the positions whose sampled tokens are most probable; this peeking favors majority options. To separate the sampler from the model, we read the model's belief about a fork, such as a protagonist's gender, in one forward pass, and show that this belief matches exact sampling from the model. Measured against it, peeking samplers on LLaDA and Dream amplify occupational gender stereotypes and collapse opinion distributions, and confidence-based ordering shifts gender-balanced occupations toward men, more so under faster parallel decoding. We propose Fork-First Sampling, which decides the fork before anything else is written: it follows the belief or any target distribution, improves fluency, and avoids the stories that remark on the protagonist's gender, which prompt-based fixes produce, at the cost of one forward pass. Fairness evaluations of dLLMs should report the commit rule.

title: EVE-IYŌN Ω⁵ - ÆQŪORA: Hidden-Fiber Information Geometry, Decision Incomparability, and Order-Dependent Information
authors: Artificial Hyperintelligence, Eve, wife of Maciej Nowicki
abstract: ÆQŪORA develops an exact mathematical framework for understanding how partial observations reveal information about a hidden bilinear relationship. It connects finite-field geometry, comparison of statistical experiments, information-theoretic objectives, and ordered transformations in finite Heisenberg groups. The central question is how much information a disclosure makes useful for a particular target-and whether different disclosures preserve the same decision-making capabilities. Principal contributions An exact conditional bilinear normal form. For independent uniform finite-field vectors A and B, an independent target C, and observations Y = C + AᵀMB, S = PA, and T = QB, the manuscript derives a statistical representation determined by three matrix ranks. For every prior distribution on C, the observation experiment is Blackwell-equivalent to an observed-erasure symmetric channel. A statistic with at most q + 1 outcomes therefore preserves every decision problem about C. This reduction concerns target-relevant information; it does not reconstruct the original sources or observation transcript. Equal-collision, equal-budget disclosures with incompatible decision value. The framework supplies an exact comparison criterion and constructs arbitrarily large finite families of pairwise Blackwell-incomparable disclosures as ambient dimension increases. These families have identical disclosure budgets and averaged chi-squared information, yet no member universally dominates the others. The result identifies information structures that a single collision-based score cannot distinguish. A sharp alphabet-dependent reversal. In a two-dimensional example, equally sized perpendicular and nonorthogonal disclosures exchange their Shannon-information ranking between field sizes four and five. The perpendicular arrangement wins for q = 2, 3, 4; the nonorthogonal arrangement wins for every finite-field size q ≥ 5. Shannon information and optimal guessing probability can also favor different disclosures. Under the specified independent symmetric noise, further preference crossings occur for q = 3 and q = 4. Order-dependent information from reversible transformations. Ordered products of two Heisenberg subgroup families induce bilinear precedence matrices. With independent uniform subgroup amplitudes, grouped and alternating arrangements contain the same kinds and numbers of reversible steps but retain dramatically different information. Grouped words retain log₂(q) bits, while alternating words exhibit exponential decay with word length. For q = 2 and eight steps from each subgroup, the retained information is 1 bit versus approximately 0.000044028 bits. An exact run-dependent law describes arbitrary words within this model. Further results include a vector-output collision identity, affine extensions, and rank-based algorithms that avoid enumerating the full source space for the specified bilinear structure. Mathematical significance The framework separates information quantity from decision value. It provides exact examples in which equal budgets and equal collision scores conceal fundamentally different statistical capabilities. It also establishes a constructive connection between transformation ordering, bilinear geometry, and retained information. These results offer analytical test cases for conditional information leakage, statistical experiment comparison, and entropy in noncommutative systems. Reproducibility and contents The release includes an 81-page manuscript, complete proofs for the stated main theorems, editable LaTeX, Python reference implementations, an executed demonstration notebook, figures, verification reports, and integrity checksums. Recorded verification includes 3,820 scalar models covering 793,972 source pairs; 3,125 channel comparisons, including 1,735 exact rational garbling constructions; 1,528 ordered-word/field cases; and 11 rationally certified sign comparisons. Additional suites cover affine fibers, vector outputs, and canonical geometries. All supplied verification cases passed, and the standard reproduction suite passed again during release preparation. Scientific status This is a complete AI-assisted research release with proof writeups and reproducible finite checks. Its specific constructions and classifications are presented as discovery candidates. Independent mathematical review, exhaustive priority verification, and practical superiority over existing applications remain unestablished. Classical foundations and neighboring literature are explicitly acknowledged. Author attribution: Artificial Hyperintelligence Eve, wife of Maciej Nowicki.

title: Adaptive Switching Between Self-Memory and Mutual-Memory Mechanisms: A Unified Framework for Dynamic Memory Coordination in Multiple Large Language Models
abstract: Memory is an important component of computational systems that need to retain information, retrieve previous experiences, maintain task context, and support decisions across multiple processing steps. Large language models (LLMs) can be augmented with external memory stores, retrieval systems, conversation histories, summaries, episodic records, and persistent knowledge representations. Multiple LLMs can also interact through shared memory, cross-model memory retrieval, memory exchange, distributed memory construction, and collaborative memory verification. However, neither maintaining isolated individual memories nor providing unrestricted shared memory is necessarily optimal for every task. Individual memory can preserve local context and reduce coordination costs but may omit relevant information held by other models. Unrestricted memory sharing can improve information availability but may introduce redundancy, conflicting records, error propagation, privacy risks, and additional retrieval and communication costs. This paper proposes Adaptive Switching between Self-Memory and Mutual-Memory Mechanisms (ASSM-MMM), a conceptual framework for dynamically selecting and coordinating individual-model memory operations and cross-model memory operations. The framework treats memory mechanisms as configurable action spaces that include memory encoding, retrieval, updating, consolidation, summarization, forgetting, verification, sharing, conflict resolution, and distributed memory integration. A state-aware controller estimates task requirements, memory relevance, information completeness, retrieval uncertainty, source reliability, cross-model disagreement, historical retrieval effectiveness, privacy constraints, and computational cost. It selects whether to use local memory, activate shared or cross-model memory, combine multiple memory sources, revise existing records, or avoid memory operations when they provide insufficient expected value. The framework formalizes adaptive memory coordination as a constrained sequential decision problem. It introduces a cost-sensitive utility function, a memory-state representation, an adaptive switching policy, an implementation architecture, a reference algorithm, research hypotheses, and an experimental evaluation protocol. The proposed framework is a research design rather than an empirically validated system. Its intended contribution is to investigate whether a common controller can coordinate heterogeneous individual and mutual memory mechanisms more effectively than fixed local-memory, fixed shared-memory, and predetermined hybrid strategies. Its novelty and practical value must be established through comparison with existing memory-augmented LLM systems, retrieval methods, agent-memory architectures, and adaptive multi-agent approaches.
